In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Sūrat al-Mu'minūn (The Believers)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾. In these verses with which He began the beginning of this sūrah, He, may He be glorified and exalted, mentioned the signs of the successful believers, so He said: ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 1], meaning: they won and attained the good of this world and the Hereafter.

The success of the believers is mentioned many times in the Qur'an, such as His saying ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is great bounty from Allah﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 47], and His saying ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 2]. The root meaning of khushū' (humble submissiveness) is stillness, tranquility, and lowering, and from it is the saying of Nābigha Dhubyānī:

"Ashes like kohl of the eye, which I make clear after a long time, and a basin-rim like the stump of a pool, broken and humbled (khāshi')."

In the sharī'ah, it is fear of Allah that resides in the heart, whose effects appear upon the limbs.

Allah counted khushū' among the attributes of those for whom He prepared forgiveness and a great reward, in His saying in al-Aḥzāb: ﴿And the humbly submissive men and the humbly submissive women﴾ up to His saying ﴿Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 35].

Here, humble submissiveness in prayer has been counted among the attributes of the successful believers who inherit al-Firdaws, and He made clear that whoever does not possess this humble submissiveness, prayer will be difficult for him, in His saying ﴿And indeed it is difficult, except for the humbly submissive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45]. A group of scholars has used His saying ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ as evidence that among the humble submissiveness of the one praying is that his gaze in prayer be directed to the place of his prostration. They said: The Prophet ﷺ used to look up to the sky during prayer, so Allah revealed ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ began to look where he prostrated.

Ṣāḥib al-Durr al-Manthūr said: Ibn Mardawayh, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan transmitted from Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, from Abū Hurayrah: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he prayed, would raise his gaze to the sky, and then ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 2] was revealed, so he lowered his head." End of quotation.

Most scholars hold that the one praying looks at the place of his prostration and does not raise his gaze. The Mālikiyyah differed from the majority, saying that the one praying looks ahead of him, not at the place of his prostration. They used as evidence His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. They said: If he looked at the place of his prostration, he would need to force himself into some kind of bowing, and that contradicts the perfection of standing. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ is that one bent with his face toward the place of his prostration is not one who has turned his face toward the Sacred Mosque. The majority is against them, as we have mentioned.

Know that the meaning of aflaḥa is: he attained falāḥ (success). Falāḥ is used in the language of the Arabs with two meanings:

The first: winning the greatest sought-after thing, and from it is the saying of Labīd:

"Then understand, if you have not yet understood, and indeed he succeeds who was given intellect."

That is, whoever was granted intellect won the greatest sought-after thing.

The second: the use of falāḥ for everlasting survival in bliss, and from it is also Labīd's saying in a rajaz of his:

"If a living being could attain falāḥ, the one who plays with spears would have attained it."

He means: attaining everlasting survival. And from this meaning is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, or al-Aḍbaṭ ibn Quray':

"For every worry among the worries there is a relief, but with the evening and the morning there is no falāḥ."

That is, there is no survival with it. There is no doubt that whoever possesses these attributes which Allah mentioned at the beginning of this noble sūrah enters Paradise, as is explicitly stated in the mentioned verses, and that whoever enters Paradise attains falāḥ in both of the two meanings mentioned, and each of the two meanings we mentioned for falāḥ. Some scholars interpreted the hadith of the adhān and iqāmah with the phrase: ḥayya 'alā al-falāḥ (hasten to success).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who turn away from vain talk﴾. In this noble verse, He - exalted is He and高 - mentioned that among the qualities of the successful believers is their turning away from vain talk (laghw). The root meaning of laghw is that which has no benefit in it, of words and deeds. It therefore includes play (la'ib), frivolity (lahw), jesting (hazl), and whatever good manners (muruwwah) require one to abandon.

Ibn Kathir said: ﴿turn away from vain talk﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3], i.e., from falsehood (batil). It includes polytheism (shirk), as some have said, and sins (ma'asi), as others have said, and whatever has no benefit in it of words and deeds. End of his quote.

What Allah praised the successful believers for in this verse, He alluded to in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]. Among their passing by it with dignity is their turning away from it and not joining its people in it. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it﴾ [al-Qasas: 55], the verse.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who are active in zakat﴾. Regarding the meaning of zakah here, there are two well-known interpretations among the scholars of knowledge:

The first: that what is meant by it is the zakat of wealth, and Ibn Kathir attributed this view to the majority.

The second: that what is meant by zakat here is the purification of the soul (zakat al-nafs), i.e., cleansing it from polytheism and sins through faith in Allah and obedience to Him and to His messengers, peace be upon them. According to this view, the meaning of zakat here is like its meaning in His saying: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it, and he has certainly failed who corrupts it﴾ [al-Shams: 9-10],

• and His saying: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-A'la: 14],

• and His saying: ﴿And if not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would ever have been pure﴾ [al-Nur: 21],

• and His saying: ﴿better than it in purity﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Kahf: 81],

• and His saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists who do not give zakah﴾ [Fussilat: 6-7],

according to one of the two interpretations. This latter view may be supported by three indications:

The first: that this surah is Meccan, without dispute, and zakat in the sense of the known zakat on wealth was prescribed in Medina, as is well known. This shows that His saying ﴿And those who are active in zakat﴾ was revealed before the prescription of the known zakat on wealth, and thus it indicates that what is meant by it is other than that.

The second indication: it is well known that when zakat on wealth is mentioned, the act of paying it is expressed by "giving" (itaa'), as in His saying: ﴿And give zakah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43] and His saying: ﴿and the giving of zakah﴾ [al-Anbiya': 73], and similar. But this zakat mentioned here is not expressed by "giving"; rather, He said concerning it: ﴿And those who are active in zakat﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 4]. This shows that this zakat is the deeds of the successful believers, and this is more fitting for the performance of acts of obedience and the abandonment of sins than the paying of wealth.

The third indication: that the zakat of wealth in the Qur'an is customarily mentioned together with prayer (salah) without any separation between them,

• such as His saying: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110],

• and His saying: ﴿and they establish prayer and give zakah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 277],

• and His saying: ﴿and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakah﴾ [al-Anbiya': 73]. Whereas the zakat mentioned here is separated from the mention of prayer by the clause ﴿And those who turn away from ill speech﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3].

Those who said that what is meant is the zakat of wealth said: the origin of zakat was prescribed in Makkah before the Hijrah, and the zakat that was prescribed in Medina in the second year is the one with the specific thresholds (nisab) and specific amounts.

We have clarified this view in al-An'am, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [al-An'am: 141]. It may be argued, since what is meant by zakah in this verse is other than the deeds by which souls are purified from the filth of polytheism and sins, that if we took the meaning of zakah as that, it would include all the attributes of the believers mentioned at the beginning of this surah, and so it would be like a repetition of them; and carrying the meaning to what is establishing and independent is preferable to other than it, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence. We have clarified this in surah al-Nahl in the discussion of His saying: ﴿So We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 97].

Those who said it is the zakat of wealth said: "active" (fa'iluna) means "those who pay" (mu'addun). They said: this is a well-known, eloquent usage, and from it is the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

"Those who feed the food in the year of hardship, and those who are active in the zakawat."

This is clear, by taking zakah in the verbal-noun sense meaning the purification of wealth, since it is the act of the one who purifies it, as is evident. And there is no doubt that the purification of the soul through deeds of righteousness and the payment of the zakat on wealth are both attributes of the successful believers who inherit Paradise.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It may be that what is meant by zakah here is the purification of the soul from polytheism and filth," until he said: "It may be that both are meant, the purification of souls and the zakat of wealth, for it is among the purification of souls, and the complete believer is the one who does this and that. And Allah knows best." End quote from him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 5 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy;﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors.﴾ In these noble verses He, exalted and high, mentions that among the attributes of the successful believers, who inherit the Paradise (Firdaws) and abide therein forever, is their guarding of their private parts, meaning from sodomy, fornication and the like. He also clarified that their guarding of their private parts is not required with respect to their women whom they have acquired enjoyment of through marriage contract or through right of possession, and what is meant by this is enjoyment of concubines. He clarified that whoever does not guard his private parts from his wife or his concubine is not blameworthy, and that whoever seeks enjoyment of his private parts beyond that, other than wives and those possessed, then he is of the transgressors (al-'adun), meaning the aggressors who exceed the limits of Allah, going beyond what Allah has made lawful to what He has forbidden.

The meaning of "al-'adun" in this verse is clarified by His saying, exalted is He, concerning the people of Lot: ﴿Do you approach males from among the worlds?﴾ ﴿And leave what your Lord has created for you of your spouses? Rather, you are a people who transgress.﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 165-166]. What He mentioned here He also mentioned in Surat Sa'ala Sa'il, because He said in it, in praise of the believers: ﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy;﴾ ﴿but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors.﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 29-31].

* *

Issues related to this noble verse

The first issue: Know that what is in His saying, ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6], is of the forms of generality (ṣīghat al-'umum), and what is intended by it is whoever... and it is of the forms of generality. The verse ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] and the verse ﴿A seeker asked﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1] indicate by their generality, the meaning indicated by the word "ma" in His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾, in both places, the permissibility of combining two sisters through right of possession by enjoying both of them together, since they are included in the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾. Dawud al-Zahiri and those who followed him held this view. But His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ [an-Nisa': 23], by its generality indicates the prohibition of combining two sisters through right of possession, because the alif and lam in "al-ukhtayn" (the two sisters) is a form of generality, encompassing every pair of two sisters, whether they are by marriage contract or by right of possession. Therefore 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was asked about combining two sisters through right of possession, said: "One verse permitted them and another verse forbade them," meaning by the permitting verse ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ and by the forbidding verse ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾.

We have explained this issue in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Illusion of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), and we will mention here, if Allah wills, the important points of what we mentioned there, and add what the need calls for adding.

The summary of the discussion on this matter is that the two mentioned verses have a partial overlap of generality (ʿumum wa khusus min wajh), in which their conflict appears to the observer in the case where they coincide, as 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "One verse permitted them and another forbade them." Its clarification is that the verse ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ stands apart from the verse ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ concerning the two sisters combined through a marriage contract, and the verse ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ stands apart concerning a single slave-woman, or two slave-women who are not sisters, and they coincide in the case of combining two sisters. So the generality of ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ requires its prohibition, and the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ requires its permissibility. When two generalities conflict in part in the case where they coincide, it is obligatory to give preference between them, and the stronger of the two is given precedence and the generality of the other is specified by it, as indicated in Maraqi al-Su'ud by his saying:

"And if the generality is partial and appears, the ruling by preference is absolutely binding."

Knowing this, be aware that the generality of ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ is preferred over the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ on five grounds:

The first of them: the generality of ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ is explicit in the place of the intended evidence in itself, because the surah is Surat an-Nisa', which is the one in which Allah clarified who is lawful among women and who is not lawful. The verse ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ in both places was not mentioned for the purpose of forbidding or permitting women; rather Allah mentioned the attributes of the believers by which they enter Paradise, and among them He mentioned guarding the private parts, then digressed to say that guarding it is not required with respect to the wife and the concubine. It is established in the principles (usul) that taking rulings from their proper sources is preferable to taking them from other than their proper sources.

The second ground: the verse ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ does not remain upon its generality by the consensus of the Muslims, because a sister by fosterage is not lawful through right of possession, by consensus, since the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is specified by the generality of ﴿and your foster sisters﴾ [an-Nisa': 23]. And the mother of one's father's concubine is not lawful through right of possession by consensus, since the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is specified by the generality of ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾ [an-Nisa': 22], and the most correct view among the usulis regarding a conflict between a general that has been specified and a general that has not been specified is to give preference to the one that has not been specified. This is the view of the majority of the usulis, and I know of no one who opposed it except Safi al-Din al-Hindi and al-Subki.

The majority's proof is that the specified general has been disputed as to whether it is a valid proof regarding what remains after the specification. Those who said it is a valid proof regarding what remains said a group of them: it is a metaphor (majaz) regarding what remains, and what is agreed upon as valid and literal (haqiqa) is that which has not been specified, which is preferable to what is disputed regarding its validity and whether it is literal or metaphorical. And even if the correct view is that it is a valid proof regarding what remains and literal in that sense, the mere occurrence of disagreement about it suffices to prefer the other over it. As for the proof of Safi al-Din al-Hindi and al-Subki for giving precedence to the one that has been specified, it is that most generals are specified, and acting on what is most common is preferable, and that what has been specified is unlikely to be specified a second time, unlike what remains upon its generality.

The third ground: the generality of ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ does not come in the context of praise or blame, whereas the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ comes in the context of praising the God-fearing. The general that comes in the context of praise or blame...

The scholars differed about treating its generality as binding. Most scholars hold that its generality is binding, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ ﴿and indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire﴾ [al-Infitar: 13-14], for it encompasses every righteous person even though it is in praise, and every wicked person even though it is in blame. Maraqi al-Su'ud says:

"What came for praise or for blame, its generality is binding according to the majority of the people of knowledge."

Some scholars disagreed in this, among them Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, saying that a general that comes in the context of praise or blame has no generality, because its intent is to encourage in praise and to deter in blame. For this reason Imam al-Shafi'i did not take the generality of His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾ [at-Tawbah: 34] to include permissible ornaments, because the verse was brought for blame, so according to him it does not include permissible ornaments.

Knowing this, be aware that the general which is not accompanied by anything preventing its generality from being binding is preferable to one accompanied by something preventing its generality from being binding, according to some scholars.

The fourth ground: even if we concede the conflict between the two verses, the default regarding private parts is prohibition, until a proof with no opposing evidence establishes permissibility.

The fifth ground: the generality that requires prohibition is preferable to that which requires permissibility, because leaving what is permissible is easier than committing what is forbidden.

These five grounds are used to refute the argument of Dawud al-Zahiri and those who followed him for permitting the combining of two sisters through right of possession, arguing from His saying: ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾. But Dawud argues from another verse, from which it is difficult to escape the argument, according to what is established in the principles of Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali jurisprudence. The clarification of this is that what is established in the principles of the three imams mentioned is that if an exception follows a series of conjoined sentences or conjoined single terms, the exception applies to all of them, unlike Abu Hanifa, who said it returns only to the last sentence. Maraqi al-Su'ud says:

"Every conjoined series that comes before the exception, all of it follows, unless there is proof from reason or from revelation..." etc.

Since you know that what is established in the principles of the three imams is that the exception returns to all the conjoined parts, and that if a waqif in his endowment deed said: "It is an endowment for the Banu Tamim, the Banu Zuhra and the poor, except the corrupt among them," the corrupt of all of them would be excluded from the endowment, since the exception returns to all, and that Abu Hanifa alone holds that it returns only to the last sentence. Therefore he did not accept the testimony of a slanderer even if he repented, reformed, and became the most upright of the people of his time, because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not accept their testimony ever after, and those are the defiant﴾ ﴿except those who repent﴾ [an-Nur: 4-5], the exception according to him returns only to the last part, which is ﴿and those are the defiant﴾, the exception ﴿except those who repent﴾ meaning that the name of defiance has departed from them, and their testimony is not accepted to be reconsidered, because of His saying ﴿and do not accept their testimony ever after﴾ except those who repent, so accept their testimony. Rather he says: "Do not accept their testimony ever after," absolutely without exception, because according to him the exception applies only to the last sentence. Abu Hanifa did not contradict his principles in His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse,﴾ up to His saying ﴿except those who repent and believe and do righteous work﴾ [al-Furqan: 68-70], for this exception returns to all the conjoined sentences before it according to Abu Hanifa and others.

But Abu Hanifa did not oppose his principle in it, because the three sentences mentioned were gathered in the final sentence, which is ﴿and whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], since the demonstrative in His saying "that" refers to shirk, killing and fornication in the conjoined sentences before it. So the final sentence included the meanings of the sentences before it, and thus the return of the exception to it alone, according to Abu Hanifa, on his established principle, entails its return to all.

Knowing this, be aware that Dawud argues for the permissibility of combining two sisters through right of possession also by the return of the exception in His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ to His saying ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾, saying: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾ and His saying ﴿and the chaste women among the women﴾ [an-Nisa': 24] both have an exception attached to each of them in His saying: ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾. So the meaning is: "And it is forbidden for you to combine two sisters, except what your right hands possess, so combining them is not forbidden for you in that case; and the married women among women are forbidden to you, except what your right hands possess, so it is not forbidden for you."

We have clarified the meaning of the exception from the married women in its proper place in this blessed book. By this you know that Dawud's argument, by the return of the exception in His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ to His saying ﴿and that you combine two sisters﴾, follows the principles of the Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis, so it is difficult for them to escape Dawud's argument.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me is that the answer to Dawud's aforementioned argument is of two aspects:

The first of these two: within the verse itself there is a clear indication that the exception does not return to His saying ﴿and that you should combine two sisters﴾, because of what we have already mentioned, that His saying ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾ means, specifically, by captivity (al-sabi) together with disbelief, and that the meaning is: "and the married women among the women [are forbidden to you], except what your right hands possess," i.e., the married women are forbidden to you, because a married woman is not lawful to anyone other than her husband, except what the right hands possess by captivity together with disbelief. For captivity removes the ruling of marriage from the captive woman, and she becomes lawful to her captor after istibra' (the waiting period to establish she is not pregnant), as al-Farazdaq said:

"And a woman with a husband whom our spears have made wed, is lawful to whoever consummates with her, if she was not divorced."

Now, if the ownership of the right hand in His saying ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾ refers specifically to captives, as is the view of the majority, then this prevents its return to His saying ﴿and that you should combine two sisters﴾, because the point of dispute concerns ownership of the right hand in general. We have already mentioned in Surat an-Nisa' that the view of whoever says ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾ is general, and that the claim that selling a slave-woman divorces her is contrary to verification, and we clarified the evidence for that.

The second aspect: the inductive study of the Qur'an indicates that the correct position regarding the return of an exception to all the conjoined sentences preceding it, or some of them, requires a separate proof, because the evidence may indicate its return to all of them or to some of them but not others. Sometimes the evidence indicates that it does not return to the nearest sentence following it. And if the exception may return to other than the sentence immediately following it, it becomes clear that one should not rule that it returns to all of them except after examining the evidence and knowing from it what is meant. This position, which is to abstain from determining whether the exception returns to all of them or to a specific part of them rather than others, except by proof, is reported from Ibn al-Hajib of the Malikis, al-Ghazali of the Shafi'is, and al-Amidi of the Hanbalis. The inductive study of the Qur'an indicates that this position is the most sound, because Allah says: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [an-Nisa': 59]. When we refer this question to Allah, we find the Qur'an indicating the soundness of this position, and by it the argument of Dawud is also refuted.

Among the verses that indicate this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation paid to his family, unless they forgo it as charity﴾ [an-Nisa': 92]. The exception returns to the compensation (diyah), so it lapses if its rightful recipient forgoes it as charity; it does not return to the freeing of the slave by unanimous agreement, because the forgoing of the compensation by its recipient does not cancel the expiation for accidental killing. Among them also is His saying: ﴿Flog them eighty lashes and do not accept their testimony ever, and those are the defiantly disobedient. Except those who repent﴾ [an-Nur: 4–5]. The exception does not return to His saying ﴿flog them eighty lashes﴾ [an-Nur: 4], because if the slanderer repents, his repentance does not remove the prescribed punishment for slander.

What is related from ash-Sha'bi, that repentance removes it, is contrary to verification, which is the position of the majority of scholars. Among them is His saying: ﴿So if they turn away, seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them a protector or a helper. Except those who join a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾ [an-Nisa': 89–90]. The exception in His saying ﴿except those who join a people﴾ does not return, by unanimous agreement, to the sentence immediately following it, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not take from among them a protector or a helper﴾ [an-Nisa': 89], because it is not permissible ever to take a protector or helper from among the disbelievers, even if they join a people between you and whom there is a covenant. Rather, the exception returns to the seizing and killing in His saying ﴿seize them and kill them﴾ [an-Nisa': 89]. The meaning is: seize them by capture and kill them, except those who join a people between you and whom there is a covenant; for you have no right to seize them by capture or to kill them, because the covenant with the people they have joined prevents their capture and killing. This was stipulated by Hilal ibn Uwaymir al-Aslami in his treaty with the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning him, Suraqa ibn Malik al-Mudlaji, and the Banu Judhayma ibn 'Amir. If the exception may not return to the nearest sentence to it in the Glorious Qur'an, which is at the highest level of inimitability, it becomes clear that it is not explicit in returning to other than it.

Among that also is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾ [an-Nisa': 83], according to what several exegetes have said, because had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy, they would have followed Satan, all of them, without exception, few or many, as you see.

They differed about the referent of this exception. It was said it returns to His saying ﴿they spread it﴾ [an-Nisa': 83]. It was said it returns to His saying ﴿those among them who would investigate it would know it﴾ [an-Nisa': 83]. And if it does not return to the sentence immediately following it, it is not explicit that it returns to other sentences.

It was also said that this exception returns to the sentence immediately following it, and that the meaning is: "And had it not been for Allah's grace upon you and His mercy by sending Muhammad (ﷺ), you would have followed Satan in persisting upon the religion of your fathers, of disbelief and the worship of idols, except a few, like those who were on the religion of Ibrahim in the Jahiliyyah, such as Zayd ibn Nufayl, Qus ibn Sa'ida, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, and their like."

Ibn Kathir mentioned that 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾ that its meaning is: you would have followed Satan, all of you. He said: the Arabs use "few" and mean by it "none." Whoever holds this view cited the saying of at-Tirimmah ibn Hakim praising Yazid ibn al-Muhallab:

"Noble, generous, with many gatherings, few in blemishes and faults."

meaning: there is no blemish in him and no fault. This view is not entirely apparent, although the Arabs do use "few" in their language to mean "none," as in their saying: "I passed through a land in which there is little leek and onion," meaning there is no leek or onion in it. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"They made their camels kneel and dropped a settlement upon a settlement; few in it are the voices except its cooing."

He means that in that wilderness there is no sound except the cooing of his she-camel. And another's saying:

"There is no harm if they returned our greeting, a little, in the sight of one who knows the truth, which disparages it."

meaning: there is no fault in it in the sight of one who knows the truth. Examples of this are many in Arabic speech. From the verses we have mentioned you know that abstaining from asserting with certainty that the exception returns to all the conjoined sentences preceding it, except with proof, is what the Qur'an indicates in several verses, and by its indication the argument of Dawud mentioned here is also refuted. And Allah knows best.

* *

The second issue: know that the scholars unanimously agreed that the ruling of this noble verse concerning enjoyment through ownership of the right hand, in His saying ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5–6], is specific to men and not women. So it is not lawful for a woman to take her male slave as a concubine and enjoy him by right of ownership. There is no disagreement among the scholars on this, and it supports the view of the majority that women are not included in the sound masculine plurals except by a separate proof, as we clarified its evidence in Surat al-Fatiha. Ibn Jarir mentioned that a woman took her slave as a concubine and said: "I interpreted a verse of the Book of Allah, ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾." So 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) was informed of it, and some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "She interpreted a verse of the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, in other than its intended sense." He said: so he struck the slave, cut off his head, and said: "You are forbidden after him to every Muslim." Then Ibn Kathir said: this is a strange, disconnected report, which Ibn Jarir mentioned in the commentary on the beginning of Surat al-Ma'ida, and it is most fitting here. He forbade her to men only, treating her with the opposite of her intent. And Allah knows best.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qurtubi said: Ma'mar narrated from Qatada, who said: a woman took her slave as a concubine, and this was mentioned to 'Umar, who asked her: "What led you to that?" She said: "I thought he was lawful for me through my right of ownership, as a woman is lawful to a man through right of ownership." 'Umar then consulted the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about stoning her. They said: "She interpreted the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, other than its intended interpretation; there is no stoning upon her." 'Umar said: "Indeed, by Allah, I will never make you lawful to any free man after him." He punished her for it, averted the prescribed penalty from her, and ordered the slave not to approach her.

From Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah, who heard his father say: I was present with 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz when a woman came to him with a young slave of hers. She said: "I took him as a concubine, but my paternal cousins prevented me from that, and I am only in the position of a man who has a slave-girl and has intercourse with her." She meant her paternal cousins. 'Umar said: "Did you marry before him?" She said: "Yes." He said: "By Allah, were it not for your standing in ignorance, I would stone you with stones. But go with him and sell him to someone who will take him out of her country." Recorded from al-Qurtubi.

* *

The third issue: know that there is no doubt that the verse ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾, namely ﴿Then whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 7], by its general meaning, prohibits masturbation by hand, known as 'amira (the act of self-stimulation), also called al-khadkhada, because whoever takes pleasure with his hand until he ejaculates his semen thereby has sought beyond what Allah has made lawful, and so he is among the transgressors by the explicit text of this noble verse mentioned here, and in Surat Sa'ala sa'il [al-Ma'arij: 1]. Ibn Kathir mentioned that ash-Shafi'i and those who followed him cited this verse as evidence for prohibiting masturbation by hand. al-Qurtubi said: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: I heard Harmala ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz say: I asked Malik about a man who performs 'amira, and he recited this verse, ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ up to His saying ﴿the transgressors﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5–7].

The one who records it, may Allah pardon and forgive him, says: What appears to me is that the argument of Malik, ash-Shafi'i, and others of the scholars from this noble verse, to prohibit 'amira, which is masturbation by hand, is a sound argument from the Book of Allah, indicated by the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and nothing has come that contradicts it from the Book or the Sunna. What is related from Imam Ahmad, despite his knowledge, eminence, and piety, permitting 'amira, reasoning by analogy that it is the expulsion of a surplus from the body which necessity calls for expelling, so it is permissible, by analogy to bloodletting and cupping, as some poet said about it:

"When you descend into a valley with no companion, perform 'amira; there is no shame or sin."

This is contrary to what is correct, even if its speaker holds the well-known station he holds, because it is an analogy that contradicts the apparent general meaning of the Qur'an, and an analogy of this kind is rejected by the defect called fasad al-i'tibar (invalidity of the consideration), as we have clarified in this blessed book many times, and we mentioned in it the words of the author of Maraqi as-Su'ud:

"Opposition to a text, or a consensus, invalidates the analogy; every one who is mindful knows this."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 5 (part 3 of 3):

So Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ and He did not make any exception from this at all except the two categories mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾. He explicitly removed blame for not guarding the private part only with regard to the wife and the female slave. Then He came with a general expression encompassing other than the two mentioned categories, indicating prohibition, which is His saying: ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 7]. Without doubt, this generality by its apparent meaning includes the one who marries his own hand (masturbation), and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an's generality may not be abandoned except by a proof from the Book or the Sunnah, which must be returned to. As for analogy (qiyas) that contradicts it, it is invalid in consideration, as we have explained. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Kathir said in his commentary on this verse, after mentioning some of those who forbade the masturbation (jald 'Umayrah) and their use of the verse as evidence, the following: "They have taken comfort in a hadith narrated by the Imam al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah in his well-known juz', where he said: 'Ali ibn Thabit al-Jazari narrated to me, from Maslamah ibn Ja'far, from Hassan ibn Humayd, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Seven whom Allah will not look at on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify, nor gather with those who work (good), and He will cause them to enter the Fire first of those who enter, unless they repent; and whoever repents, Allah will accept his repentance (p-318): the one who marries his own hand, the doer and the one done to, the habitual drinker of wine, the one who strikes his parents until they cry for help, the one who harms his neighbours until they curse him, and the one who marries his neighbour's wife."'" End of quote.

Then Ibn Kathir said: "This is a gharib hadith, and its chain contains one who is not known, due to his unknown status. And Allah knows best." End of his words. However, despite its weakness, the apparent meaning of the Qur'an in general bears witness to it regarding marrying the hand, by its indication of prohibiting that. The reason it is called "jald 'Umayrah" for masturbation is that they use "'Umayrah" as a euphemism for the male organ.

A subtle point: it is mentioned in the "Anecdotes of the Heedless" (Nawadir al-Mughaffalin) that a heedless man whose mother owned a female slave named 'Umayrah once beat her, so the slave cried out. A group of people heard her cries, came and said: "What is this screaming?" That heedless man said to them: "No harm; that is my mother beating 'Umayrah."

* *

The fourth issue: Know that we have previously mentioned in Surah al-Nisa' that this verse, which is His saying: ﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾, indicates by its apparent meaning the prohibition of temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah), because He, exalted is He, stated in it what implies the obligation to guard the private part from anyone other than the wife and the concubine. Then He explicitly stated that the one who seeks beyond that is among the transgressors by His saying: ﴿But whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors.﴾ And the woman enjoyed in temporary marriage is neither a wife nor a slave. As for her not being a slave, it is clear. As for the evidence that she is not a wife, it is the absence of the necessary consequences of marriage from her, such as inheritance, the waiting period ('iddah), divorce, maintenance, and the like. For if she were a wife, she would inherit, observe the 'iddah, be subject to divorce, and be owed maintenance. Since the necessary consequences of marriage are absent from her, we know she is not a wife, because the negation of the necessary implies the negation of what necessitates it, by the consensus of rational people.

Thus it becomes clear that the one who seeks temporary marriage is among the transgressors who exceed what Allah has permitted to what He has forbidden. We have clarified this in Surah al-Nisa' with proofs from the Book and the Sunnah, and that temporary marriage is prohibited until the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of the word "'ala" (upon) in this verse may be obscure to the student of knowledge, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives﴾, etc.; because the root of guarding (hifz) does not, in this context, take a second object with "'ala." So it is said: "'ala" here means "'an" (from).

The meaning: they guard their private parts from everything, except from their wives. And hafiza may take "'an."

Al-Zamakhshari tried to answer the use of "'ala" here, and said the following: "'Ala azwajihim" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), i.e., "except as governors over their wives," or "as guardians over them," from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so; he died leaving her, and so-and-so succeeded to her," and its parallel: "Ziyad was over Basra," meaning governing it. From this is the saying: "So-and-so is under so-and-so," and from this the woman was called a "bed" (firash).

The meaning: they guard their private parts in all circumstances, except in their marriage or their taking of concubines; or "'ala" is attached to a deleted element indicated by "ghayru maluminin" (not blameworthy), as if it were said: "they are blamed, except concerning their wives," i.e., they are blamed for every intercourse except what is permitted to them, for they are not blameworthy for it. Or you make it a complement to "hafizun" from your saying: "Guard over me the reins of my horse," by implying the meaning of negation, just as the saying "I adjure you by Allah, except you do it" is construed as meaning "I did not request from you anything but your doing it." End of his words. And what is in it of lack of clarity is not hidden.

Abu Hayyan said: These aspects which al-Zamakhshari strained after show clear signs of being non-Arabic (ujmah), and they are contrived. Then Abu Hayyan inclined to the view that the statement is of the type of implication (tadmin): "hafizun" is implied to mean "mumsikun" (restraining) or "qasirun" (confining), and both take "'ala," as in His saying: ﴿Keep your wife upon you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. The apparent meaning is that His saying here, ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾, although the owned ones are among rational beings and rational beings are referred to by "man" not "ma," is because the female slaves, since they have some attributes of non-rational beings, such as being sold and bought and the like, this justified using the word "ma" for them. And Allah knows best.

Some scholars said: "Wara' dhalika" is the object of "ibtagha," meaning "sought other than that." Some of them said: the direct object is elided, and "wara'" is an adverbial of place, meaning: "whoever seeks, enjoying his private part, beyond that."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 8:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who are, to their trusts and their covenant, observant﴾. In this noble verse, He - majestic and exalted - mentioned that among the attributes of the successful believers who inherit Paradise (al-Firdaws) is that they are observant of their trusts and their covenant, i.e., they guard the trusts and the covenants. The trust (amanah) includes everything that God has entrusted you with and commanded you to preserve, so it includes guarding your limbs from everything that does not please God, and guarding what you have been entrusted with of the rights of people. The covenants (ʿuhud) also include everything over which a pledge has been taken from you to preserve, of the rights of God and the rights of people. The guarding of trusts and covenants contained in this noble verse is explained in many verses;

• like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa' 58]

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger or betray your trusts while you know [the truth]﴾ [al-Anfal 27]

• and His saying, may He be exalted, concerning the one who asked: ﴿And those who are, to their trusts and their covenant, observant﴾ [al-Ma'arij 32]

• and His saying concerning the covenant: ﴿And fulfill the covenant. Indeed, the covenant is ever [that about which one will be] questioned﴾ [al-Isra' 34]

• and His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fulfill [your] contracts﴾, the verse [al-Ma'idah 1]

• and His saying: ﴿And whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah - He will give him a great reward﴾ [al-Fath 10]

• and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you have taken it﴾ [an-Nahl 91]. We have clarified this in Surah al-Anbiya' in the discussion of His saying ﴿And [mention] David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field﴾, the verse [al-Anbiya' 78].

As for His saying, ra'un (observant): it is the sound plural of ra'i (guardian), who is one who is in charge of a thing, by preserving or reforming it, like the shepherd of sheep (ra'i al-ghanam) and the leader of the subjects (ra'i al-ra'iyyah). And in the hadith: "Each of you is a shepherd (ra'in) and each of you is responsible for his flock," the hadith [continues]. Ibn Kathir alone read this letter: li-amanatihim (in the singular, without an alif after the nun), in the form of the singular, while the rest read it with an alif after the nun, in the form of the sound feminine plural.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And those who are attentive to their prayers,﴾ In this noble verse, He - exalted is He - mentioned that among the attributes of the successful believers who inherit Paradise (al-Firdaws) is that they guard their prayers (yuhafizuna 'ala salawatihim). Guarding them includes completing their pillars (arkan), their conditions (shurut), and their sunan, performing them at their proper times, and performing them in congregation in the mosques. Because this is among the causes of attaining al-Firdaws, He, exalted is He, commanded guarding them in His saying: ﴿Guard the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], to the end of the verse. He, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Ma'arij: ﴿And those who are attentive to their prayers﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 34], and He also said in it: ﴿Except those who pray, who are constant in their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 22-23]. He censured and threatened those who did not guard them in His saying: ﴿Then there succeeded them an evil generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will meet deception (ghayy)﴾ [Maryam: 59].

We have clarified this in Surat "Maryam," and in His saying: ﴿So woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Ma'un: 4-5]. He, exalted is He, said in censuring the hypocrites: ﴿And when they stand to prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to the people﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 142]. And in the Sahih (of al-Bukhari and Muslim), on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud - may Allah be pleased with him - that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which deed is most beloved to Allah?" He said: "Prayer at its appointed time," (p-321) the hadith... We have already presented it. The narrations on the virtue of prayer and of guarding it are very numerous, but the subject of our book is the explanation of the Qur'an by the Qur'an, and we generally do not mention explanation from the Sunnah except when the Qur'an's explanation is not sufficient for the intended meaning, in which case we complete the explanation from the Sunnah, as we have presented many times and mentioned in the introduction of this blessed book.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit the Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾. In this noble verse, He, may He be exalted and majestic, mentioned that the believers who possess the qualities we have previously mentioned are "the inheritors." He omitted the object of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), which is "the inheritors" (al-warithun), because of the indication of His saying: ﴿who will inherit the Firdaws﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 11] upon it. Al-Firdaws is the highest and middle part of Paradise, from which the rivers of Paradise gush forth, and above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, may He be exalted. Here He, may He be exalted, expressed attaining al-Firdaws by the term "inheritance."

We have already clarified the meaning of inheritance and the verses that indicate that meaning, such as:

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is the Garden which We cause to inherit from among Our servants whoever was God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 63]

• His saying: ﴿And they are called out: "This is the Garden which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do."﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the land, to settle in Paradise wherever we will"﴾ [al-Zumar: 74], and the verse, in the discussion of His saying in Surat Maryam: ﴿That is the Garden which We cause to inherit from among Our servants whoever was God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 63], which suffices instead of repeating it here.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this letter (in the word ṣalawātihim, "their prayers") as ʿalā ṣalātihim, without a waw, in the singular form. The rest read ʿalā ṣalawātihim [al-Mu'minun: 9], with an open waw, in the sound feminine plural form. The meaning is one, because the singular noun which is a noun of genus (ism jins), when it is annexed to a definite noun, becomes a form of generality, as is well known in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh).

His saying here: ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾ means: without cessation, forever, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿a gift not cut off﴾ [Hud: 108], meaning not cut off. He, may He be exalted, also said: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad: 54], and He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿What is with you will be exhausted, and what is with God is lasting﴾ [al-Nahl: 96].

As we have already presented in full.

The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 12:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay﴾ ﴿Then We made him a drop [of fluid] in a firm place﴾ ﴿Then We made the drop a clinging clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾. In this noble verse, He, exalted is He, explained the stages of His creation of man and His transferring him from state to state, so that His creation thereby would show the perfection of His power and His deserving to be worshipped alone, exalted is He. We have already clarified in (p-322) the beginning of Surah al-Hajj the meaning of nutfah (drop), 'alaqah (clot), and mudghah (lump), and we explained the views of the scholars regarding the formed (mukhallaqah) and the unformed (ghayr mukhallaqah), and the correct position on that. We also clarified the rulings regarding pregnancy when it miscarries as a clot or a lump: whether the waiting period of the pregnant woman is concluded by it or not;

and whether a slave-woman becomes an umm walad (mother of a child) by it if it is from her master or not; and other rulings concerning the miscarried fetus, when it inherits and is inherited from, and when the funeral prayer is offered over it, and the views of the scholars on these matters, in the discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust﴾ and the verses that follow [al-Hajj: 5]. Here we will mention what we did not explain there, along with the verses related to this meaning. As for the meaning of sulalah (extract): it is fu'alah, from "salaltu al-shay' min al-shay'," when you extract it from it. From this is the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

Ⅰ He created creation from the extract of a foul one, and to the extract all of them will return.

The child is the sulalah of his father, as if he slipped out from his father's back.

From it is the saying of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

Ⅰ So she brought him forth, a strong-hided lion-cub, the extract of a vagina that was not fortified.

The pattern of the noun as fu'alah indicates paucity, like qulamat al-zufr (paring of the nail) and nuhatat al-shay' al-mankut (shavings of a carved thing), which is what falls from it during carving. The meaning of creating man from an extract of clay is the creation of their father Adam from it, as He said: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59].

We have previously clarified the stages of that dust: that when it was moistened with water it became ṭayyib, and when it was left to ferment it became lazib clay that sticks to the hand, and became ḥama' masnun. Some said: black, foul clay; and some said: masnun means shaped, as its explanation was already given in Surah al-Hijr. Then, when He created him from clay, He created from him his spouse Hawwa', as He said at the beginning of An-Nisa': ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from one soul and created from it its mate﴾ [An-Nisa': 1], and He said in al-A'raf: ﴿and made from it its mate﴾ [al-A'raf: 189], and He said in az-Zumar: ﴿then made from it its mate﴾ [az-Zumar: 6], as all of that was previously clarified. Then, when He created the man and the woman, the existence of the human species from them was through procreation, so the first of its stages is the drop, then the clot, etc.

We have explained most of this at the beginning of Surah al-Hajj. His saying here: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12] means: He began the creation of the human species with the creation of Adam. His saying ﴿Then We made him a drop﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13], i.e., after the creation of Adam and Hawwa'. The pronoun in His saying "Then We made him" (p-323) refers to the human species, which is the offspring, by the indication of the context, like their saying: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning: and half of another dirham. Allah, exalted is He, clarified this meaning in Surah as-Sajdah in His saying: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ ﴿who perfected everything He created and began the creation of man from clay﴾ ﴿then made his offspring from an extract of a despised fluid﴾ ﴿then proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful﴾ [as-Sajdah: 6–9]. He alluded to this with His saying: ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust; then, behold, you are human beings dispersed﴾ [ar-Rum: 20]. What He mentioned here of the stages of His creation of man, He commanded every accountable person to reflect upon, and an absolute command requires obligation unless there is a diverting proof, as we have explained repeatedly. That is in His saying: ﴿So let man observe from what he was created﴾ ﴿He was created from a gushing fluid﴾ — the verse [at-Tariq: 5–6]. He has indicated in many verses to the perfection of His power by transferring man through the stages of his creation from stage to stage, as He clarified here; and as in His saying: ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not attribute to Allah [due] grandeur?﴾ ﴿while He has created you in stages﴾ [Nuh: 13–14]. He made clear that the turning away of people from reflecting on this and taking lesson from it is something that warrants wonder and astonishment, and that among the wonders of His workmanship and marvels of His power is His transferring man from a drop to a clot, and from a clot to a lump, etc., although he did not split his mother's belly; rather he is concealed within three darknesses: the darkness of the womb, the darkness of the uterus, and the darkness of the placenta enveloping the fetus. This is in His saying, exalted and high is He: ﴿He creates you within the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs sovereignty. There is no deity except Him, so how are you turned away?﴾ [az-Zumar: 6]. So contemplate the meaning of His saying ﴿so how are you turned away?﴾, i.e., away from these wonders and marvels which your Lord and your Worshipped One has done in you. And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿It is He who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6], and He said: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clot, then from a lump, formed and unformed﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. Then He mentioned the wisdom, saying ﴿that We may make clear to you﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], i.e., that We may manifest to you thereby Our greatness, the perfection of Our power, Our singularity in divinity, and the entitlement to worship. He said in Surah al-Mu'min: ﴿It is He who created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clot, then brings you out as a child, then [lets you reach] your maturity, then [lets you become] elders﴾ [Ghafir: 67]. And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ ﴿Then he became a clot, and [Allah] created and proportioned﴾ ﴿and made of him two mates, the male and the female﴾ ﴿Is not He [who does that] Able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36–40]. Verses similar to this are many. He left these mentioned stages vague in His saying (p-324): ﴿No! Indeed, We created them from that which they know﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 39], and this vagueness indicates their weakness and the greatness of their Creator, exalted is He. So glorified is He, exalted is He; how great is His station, how perfect is His power, and how manifest are the proofs of His oneness.

In this verse of al-Mu'minun He has explained that He makes the lump into bones, and He explained in another place that He assembles some of those bones with others with strong assembly, and binds some of them to others, in the most perfect and wondrous manner. This is in His saying: ﴿We created them and strengthened their joints﴾ [al-Insan: 28]. Al-asr is the binding of bones to one another; and ta'asir of the saddle and the woman's riding-litter are the thongs by which it is tied. From it is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:

Ⅰ And she did not enter the sharp trot until the bindings of the upper part of her saddle-girth were loosened and broken.

In the Sihah of al-Jawhari: "Asara qatabahu ya'siruhu asran": he tied its saddle with the asar, which is the qadd (rawhide strip), and from it the captive (asir) got his name, for they used to bind him with qadd. So the saying of some exegetes and lexicographers, "asrahum, i.e., their creation had deficiency in it," is an imperfect explanation; because asr is strong binding with the asar which is the qadd, a strip cut from the hide of a camel or the like that has not been tanned. Allah, exalted is He, binds some bones to others, binding them firmly and cohesively as one binds a thing with qadd, and binding with it is very strong.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿in a firm place﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 13]: qarar here means the place of settling, and makkin means the one that is firmly established. He described the qarar with it because of its firmness in itself such that no disorder befalls it, or because of the firmness of whoever resides in it. Abu Hayyan said this in al-Bahr. Al-Zamakhshari said: qarar means the settled place, and what is meant by it is the womb, which is described with the firmness that is the attribute of one settled in it, or with its firmness in itself, since it has been made firm in such a way that it is secured.

His saying in this verse: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., a creation completely distinct from the first creation, with a distinction how far it is: He made him living when he was inanimate, speaking when he was mute, hearing when he was deaf, seeing when he was blind; and He placed within him and without him, and every organ of his and part of his is a wonder of natural design and a marvel of wisdom which is not grasped by the description of the describer nor by the explanation of the explainer. End of his words.

Al-Qurtubi said: There is disagreement about the other creation mentioned. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: "It is the breathing of the spirit into him after he had been inanimate." And from Ibn 'Abbas: "his coming out into this world." Qatadah said: "the sprouting of his hair." Al-Dahhak said: "the emergence of teeth and the growth of hair." Mujahid said: "the completion of his youth." It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar... and the correct view is that it is general to all of this and to other things, of speech, perception, and the acquisition of intellectual understandings, until he dies. End of his words.

(p-325) The apparent meaning is that all the views of the scholars regarding His saying "another creation" are that he became a complete human after having been a drop, a lump, a clot, and bones, as is evident.

* *

A Question

This verse has been used by Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, as evidence that whoever usurps an egg, and it hatches in his possession, he is liable for the egg and does not return the chick, because the chick is a creation other than the egg; it is other than what was usurped, and the usurper only returns what he usurped. This argument has a certain basis in reasoning, and Allah knows best.

His saying in this verse: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. And His saying ﴿So blessed is Allah﴾: Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr al-Muhit: tabaraka is a past-tense verb that is not inflected, and its meaning is: exalted and sanctified. End of his words.

His saying in this verse ﴿the best of creators﴾ — i.e., the ones who determine (muqaddirin), for the Arabs use "khalq" meaning "taqdir" (measuring/determining). From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

Ⅰ Indeed you execute what you have determined, while some of the people determine but do not execute.

His saying "yakhluqu thumma la yafri" means: he determines the matter, then does not carry it out, due to his inability to do so, as is known. It is also known that the grammarians differ regarding the superlative form when it is added to a definite noun: whether its idafah is a pure (mahḍah) idafah or a non-pure verbal (lafziyyah) idafah, as is well known in its place. Whoever says it is pure parses His saying "ahsanu al-khaliqin" as an adjective (na't) for the word of majesty (Allah); and whoever says it is non-pure parses it as an apposition (badal). It has also been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: He is the best of creators. He read these two letters: ﴿and We created the lump as bones﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14] and His saying ﴿then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾: Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah from 'Asim read "'azman" with a fatha on the 'ayn and sukun on the za' without alif, in singular form in both places; and the rest read "'izaman" with kasra on the 'ayn and fatha on the za', and an alif after it, in plural form. On the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah, the intended meaning of "'azm" is "'izam."

We have already explained in detail at the beginning of Surah al-Hajj and elsewhere that if the singular is a noun of genus (ism jins), the Arabs may use it while meaning the plural, and we gave many examples of this in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech, with its definiteness, indefiniteness and idafah; so that suffices and need not be repeated here.

(p-326) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then indeed you, after that, are surely going to die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised up.﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Exalted, explains that after He has brought them into being as another creation, He brings forth each one of them from his mother's womb as a child; then he becomes one who has reached puberty (muhtalim), then a young man, then a middle-aged man (kahl), then an elder (shaykh), then one of decrepit old age (haram), and that they all are heading toward death, whether they are granted a long life or not. Then, after death, they will be raised up alive on the Day of Resurrection for reckoning (hisab) and recompense (jaza'). This death and life mentioned here each has another counterpart, because they are two deaths and two lives; one of each is mentioned here, and all of them are mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die; then He will bring you to life again﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28], and His saying: ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice and You have given us life twice"﴾ [Ghafir: 11], as we have already explained in Surat al-Hajj and al-Baqarah. All of this is evidence of His perfect power, the obligation of faith in Him, and His right to be worshipped alone, glorified be He and exalted far above what they say.

The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And We have created above you seven paths, and We were never unmindful of creation﴾ (17). Regarding His words, Exalted, "ṭarā'iq" (طَرَائِقَ, "paths"), there are two possible interpretations (tafsir):

The first: it is called "ṭarā'iq" because some of it is above other parts of it, from their saying ṭāraqa al-na'l (طَارَقَ النَّعْلَ), meaning when he made it into layers (ṭāq) upon layers, and assembled some of it upon others. From this is His Messenger's (ﷺ) saying (ﷺ), "Their faces were like shields layered (al-majānn al-muṭraqah)," meaning shields that were made with layers, some above others. From this is the poet's verse describing a sandal of his that had layers:

"And layered sandals behind them, falling, the desert twists with them."

He means the sandals of camels. From this is their saying: "a bird with layered feathers (ṭarrāq al-rīsh)," and muṭraqah, when some of its feathers are placed over others. From this is Zuhayr's verse describing a falcon:

"It swoops upon her, dark-cheeked, with feathers layered over its primary feathers, for which no nets were set."

And Dhu al-Rummah's verse, also describing a falcon:

"Layered in its secondary feathers, lying over its back, the dew of its night glistening in its feathers."

And another's verse describing a sandgrouse:

"Pale-white, bound in her feathers are layered markings, black are her primary feathers, her secondary feathers dulled."

According to this view, His words "seven paths" are clarified by His words: "Do you not see how Allah created seven heavens in layers?" (Nuh: 15), and this is the view of the majority.

The second: it is called "ṭarā'iq" because they are the routes of the angels in descent and ascent. It has also been said: because they are the paths of the stars in their courses. As for the view of one who said it is called "ṭarā'iq" because each heaven has a path and a form different from the others, and the view of one who said "ṭarā'iq" means "spread out," both are clearly far-fetched.

As for His words, "And We were never unmindful of creation" (al-Mu'minun: 17), we have already mentioned that its meaning is like His words: "And He holds back the heaven from falling upon the earth" (al-Hajj: 65), because whoever holds the heaven, if He were heedless, it would fall and destroy creation, as its clarification has already been explained. Some have said: "And We were never unmindful of creation," rather, We are the ones who maintain the reform of all their affairs and facilitate everything they need. And His words, "And We have created above you seven paths," meaning the heavens, are a proof for His words before it: "Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be resurrected" (al-Mu'minun: 16), because whoever is able to create the heavens, despite their greatness, there is no doubt that He is able to create man, as in His words: "The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind" (Ghafir: 57), and His words: "Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He constructed it..." (al-Nazi'at: 27), and His words: "Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?" (Ya-Sin: 81). The verses with this meaning are numerous.

We have already presented the proofs of resurrection, of which this proof is one, and we gave many examples of them; they are mentioned here, but we did not elaborate on them here because we have clarified them previously in al-Nahl and al-Baqarah. And Allah knows best.

(p-٣٢٧)

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky in a measured amount, and We caused it to settle in the earth; and indeed, We are able to take it away.﴾ In this noble verse, He mentions that He sent down water from the sky, using the plural form, which is intended to express majesty, glorifying Himself, may He be exalted. That water which He sent down from the sky He caused to settle in the earth so that people may benefit from it in wells, springs, and the like. He, may He be exalted, is able to take it away, and if He willed to take it away, all creation would perish from the loss of water at its source, through hunger and thirst. He made clear that He sent it down "in measure," meaning in a specific quantity with Him, by which the creatures benefit, and which He does not increase for them to the point where it would be like the flood of Noah, lest it destroy them. He sends it down in the amount in which there is benefit and not harm. Glory be to Him, may He be exalted; how great He is and how great is His gentleness toward His creation. These three matters that He mentioned in this noble verse are explained elsewhere.

(p. 328) The first is that He sends it down "in measure," which He pointed to in His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures, and We do not send it down except in a known measure.﴾ [al-Hijr: 21].

The second is His causing the water sent down from the sky to settle in the earth, which He explained in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky and makes it flow as springs in the earth?﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The yanbu' (spring) is abundant water. And His saying: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky, and We gave you to drink from it, and you are not its keepers.﴾ [al-Hijr: 22], as we have already discussed in the commentary on al-Hijr.

The third is His power to take it away, to which He pointed in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should sink away, who would bring you clear water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30]. Its meaning is similar to His saying: ﴿If We willed, We could make it bitter; so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70], because when it becomes salty and bitter, drinking from it is impossible and benefiting from it is impossible, so it is in the status of the non-existent. He has explained how He sends down water from the sky in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap, and you see the rain coming out from their midst?﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. He clearly stated that the rain (al-wadq), which is the downpour, comes out from among the clouds (al-sahab), which is the muzn (cloud), and it is the vessel in which the water is. He also explained that the cloud fills with water until it becomes heavy because of the great amount of water in it, in His saying: ﴿Until, when they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land﴾, the verse [al-A'raf: 57]. So His saying "thiqal" is the plural of "thaqilah" (heavy), and its heaviness is only due to the water in it. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12] is the plural of "sahabah thaqilah" (a heavy cloud).

These Qur'anic verses indicate that Allah gathers the water in the muzn, then brings it out from among the clouds. Khilal (among) of a thing means its openings and gaps that are not closed. He, may He be exalted, has made clear that it is He who sends it down and directs it among His creatures as He wills. So He sends abundant rain to the lands of one people for a year, until fertility abounds in them and blessings increase, in order to test its people in giving thanks for the blessing. And does He see whether they take heed of the greatness of the sign in the sending down of water? And He sends little rain upon them in some years, so their livestock perish from drought, their crops do not grow, and their trees do not bear fruit, so as to test them thereby: will they repent to Him and return to what pleases Him?

He made clear that, along with His general favor upon the creatures by sending down rain in the beneficial measure and causing its water to settle in the earth so that they and their cattle may drink from it and benefit from it, most of them refuse except disbelief in it. This is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ ﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land and give drink to much of what We have created of cattle and people﴾ ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them that they may remember, but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ [al-Furqan: 48–50].

(p. 329) Without doubt, among those who refused except disbelief are those who claim that the rain was not sent down by a sender who is an active, choosing agent, but rather that it fell by its own nature. So the one who sends it down, in their view, is nature. And the nature of water is evaporation: when the degrees of heat from the sun or from friction with the wind accumulate upon it, that vapor rises by its nature, then gathers, then condenses, and that condensation is a natural matter with no agent, and that is the rain. Thus they deny Allah's blessing in His sending down the rain, and they deny the evidence in its sending down for the power of the One who sends it down, and the obligation of faith in Him, and His deserving to be worshipped alone. Such people are included in His saying: ﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief﴾, after His saying: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them that they may remember﴾.

In His saying "And We have certainly distributed it," He has stated clearly that He, may He be exalted, is the one who directs the water and sends it down wherever He wills and however He wills. Of the same kind as this meaning is what is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in the dawn prayer at al-Hudaybiyah, following a night rain. When he finished, he turned to the people and said: 'Do you know what your Lord said?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'He said: "This morning among My servants there are those who believe in Me and those who disbelieve in Me. As for the one who said: We have been given rain by the grace of Allah and His mercy, he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the star. As for the one who said: We have been given rain by such-and-such a nawʼ (star-setting), he is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the star."'" This is the wording of Muslim, may Allah have mercy on him, in his Sahih. Without doubt, whoever says "We have been given rain by the vapor of such-and-such," attributing it to nature, is a disbeliever in Allah and a believer in nature and vapor. The Arabs used to claim that some of the rain originates from the sea, yet they attributed the action to the active, choosing Agent, may He be exalted. Among their poetry on this is the saying of Tarafah ibn al-'Abd:

Do not blame me, for they are women of sleep in summer, with short, thin, fine-haired veils,
Like the daughters of the sea, moist, when summer has made the green shoots grow tall.

So his saying "daughters of the sea" means the clouds (al-muzn) whose water originates from the sea.

And the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

May there water every last night for Umm 'Amr clouds, bright, whose water is pouring forth,
They drank from the water of the sea, then rose up, and in them are dark seas with their roaring.

Without doubt, the Creator of the heavens and the earth, may He be exalted, is the One who sends down rain in the measure that He wills, however He wills, glory be to Him and exalted is He above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 19:

(p-330) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens of date palms and grapevines; in them you have abundant fruit, and from them you eat.﴾ We have already presented the clear verses concerning what this noble verse indicates in Surat an-Nahl, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the date palms, and the grapevines﴾ [an-Nahl: 11], and others. That suffices, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 20:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, producing oil and a relish for those who eat﴾. His saying "shajaratan" (a tree) is in apposition (ma'tuf) to "jannatin" (gardens), being the coordination of the specific upon the general (ʿatf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm). We have mentioned its justification many times.
