That is: We brought forth for you gardens by it, and We brought forth for you by it a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, and it is the olive tree, as He, may He be exalted, indicated by His saying: ﴿It is lit from a blessed tree, an olive tree﴾ [al-Nur: 35], and so on. The oil by which it grows is its oil mentioned in His saying: ﴿whose oil would almost glow﴾ [al-Nur: 35], along with the light derived from it. So it is "sibgh" (a relish) for those who eat, that is, a condiment with which they dip their food.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu ʿAmr read "Sina'" (سيناء) with a kasra on the sin, while the rest read it with a fatha. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "tunbitu" (تُنْبِتُ) with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ba' (the present tense of the causative form "anbata", the fourth form verb), while the rest read "tanbutu" (تَنْبُتُ) with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the ba' (the present tense of the basic form "nabata", the first form verb). On this reading there is no difficulty with the letter "ba'" (bi) in His saying "bi-al-duhn" (with the oil), meaning: it grows accompanied by the oil extracted from its olives. But on the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr, there is a difficulty with the "ba'", namely that "anbata" (the causative fourth form) is transitive in itself and does not need the "ba'". We have already explained the point regarding the use of such a "ba'" in the Qur'an, and we have given many examples of it in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs, in the discussion of His saying in surah Maryam: ﴿And shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ [Maryam: 25] and so on. It should not be unclear that the causative fourth form, according to the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr here, is intransitive (lazima) and not transitive in its object, whereas "anbata" is transitive, and it is sometimes intransitive. Its transitive use appears in His saying: ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops and the olives﴾ [al-Nahl: 11], and His saying: ﴿So We caused to grow thereby gardens and grain of harvest﴾ [Qaf: 9]. Its intransitive use is the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr mentioned above. A parallel in the speech of the Arabs is the verse of Zuhayr:

*I saw those in need around their tents, dwelling there, until, when the herbage grew (anbata al-baql)...*

So his saying "anbata al-baql" is intransitive, meaning "nabata". This is the correct view regarding the reading "tunbitu" with a damma on the ta', contrary to those who said it is the present tense of the transitive "anbata", with an implied object, that is: "tunbitu zaytunaha" (it causes its olives to grow), and in it is the oil.

Ibn Kathir said: "al-Tur" is the mountain. Some of them said: it is only called "tur" if there are trees on it; if it is bare of trees, it is called a "jabal" (mountain), not a "tur". And Allah knows best. And Tur Sina' is Tur Sinin, the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Musa ibn ʿImran, peace be upon him, and the mountains around it, in which there are olive trees. End of Ibn Kathir's relevant words.

In the hadith of Abu Usayd Malik ibn Rabi'ah al-Sa'idi al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Eat the oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree." Narrated by Ahmad, and narrated by al-Tirmidhi and others from ʿUmar. The apparent view is that it is not free from criticism. al-ʿAjluni said of it in Kashf al-Khafa' wa Muzil al-Ilbas: "Narrated by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah from ʿUmar, and Ibn Majah alone from Abu Hurayrah, and al-Hakim declared it sound according to the conditions of both of them. Then he said: and there are similar reports from a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all." End of quotation from him. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you: We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾. We have already presented the verses that clarify the meaning of this verse, and the legal rulings (al-ahkam al-fiqhiyyah) derived from it, in surah an-Nahl, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you: We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾ [an-Nahl: 66], together with an explanation of the modes of recitation (awjuh al-qira'ah). That suffices, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾. The pronoun in His saying "upon them" refers to the cattle (al-an'am) mentioned in His saying: ﴿And indeed for you in the cattle﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 21]. In this verse He, may He be exalted, has made clear that He carries His creation upon the cattle, and what is meant here by them is the camels, because being carried upon them is the most common. "Upon the ship": these are the ships (sufun). The word "al-fulk" (ship) is applied to both the singular and the plural of ships. What He, may He be exalted, mentioned in this noble verse of the favours He bestowed upon His creation by making riding and carrying easy for them, upon the cattle and the ships, has come clarified in other verses,

• such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah is the One who made for you the cattle that you may ride some of them and from some of them you eat﴾ ﴿And for you in them are benefits, and that you may reach upon them a need in your breasts, and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ [Ghafir: 79-80].

• And His saying concerning the cattle: ﴿Have they not seen that We created for them, from what Our hands have done, cattle, so they are their owners?﴾ ﴿And We subjugated them for them, so some of them are their mounts and from some of them they eat﴾ [Ya-Sin: 71-72].

• And His saying concerning them: ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with difficulty to the souls. Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 7].

• And His saying concerning the ship and the cattle together: ﴿And who created all the pairs and made for you of the ships and cattle that which you ride﴾ ﴿That you may sit upon their backs and then remember the favour of your Lord when you have settled upon them and say, "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we were not able to do it. And indeed, to our Lord we will return."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 12-14].

• And His saying concerning the ships: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ ﴿And We created for them from its likeness that which they ride﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41-42]. And His saying: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you what is in the earth and the ship running through the sea by His command?﴾ [al-Hajj: 65].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you see the ship therein plowing through, that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Nahl: 14].

Verses of this kind are many, and this is among His blessings and signs. He joined the cattle with the ships in the mentioned verses because camels are "ships of the land," as Dhu al-Rummah said:

Unquestioningly, she appeared to me while my companions slept, and only her greeting roused the drowsy one, arriving at night.

And the saddle-cords fastened to her, a ship of the land, her reins beneath my cheek.

So you see that he named his she-camel "a ship of the land." And "julab al-rahl" (the saddle-frame), with a dammah or kasrah on the jim, are its wooden parts, or the saddle together with what is in it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah﴾ up to His saying ﴿nor can they delay [it]﴾. The indications regarding what it contains of signs have already been given, and these have explanation in many other places, so this makes repeating them here unnecessary.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him, so We made them follow one another [to destruction], and We made them into tales. So away with a people who do not believe.﴾ In this noble verse, He, may He be exalted, explains that after the sending of Nuh and the messenger mentioned after him, He sent His messengers tatra (in succession), i.e., consecutively, one after another. Every thing that follows in continuous succession, the Arabs call mutawatir (successive), and from this is the saying of Labid in his Mu'allaqa:

؎ It rises along the path of its ridge, a successive [cloud] in a night whose clouds concealed the stars.

He means: continuous rain, or a continuous dust-storm of wind. The tā' in tatrā is substituted from a wāw. And [the meaning is] that whenever He sent a messenger to a nation, they denied him, and so He destroyed them, and He made some follow others into complete annihilation because of their denial of the messengers. This meaning mentioned in this noble verse is explained in many verses. The verse that makes an exception of one nation from this destruction mentioned has also been clarified.

As for the verses that clarify what this verse indicates, they are very numerous:

• Like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not send a warner into any town but its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ [Saba': 34],

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We did not send before you a warner into any town but its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 23],

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not send into any town a prophet but that We seized its people with adversity and hardship that they might humble themselves.﴾ ﴿Then We exchanged the bad state for good until they had multiplied [in numbers] and said, "Hardship and ease had touched our fathers," and We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-A'raf: 94–95], the verse.

And verses like this are very numerous.

As for the verse that clarifies the exception of one nation from these nations, it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed and its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the worldly life﴾ [Yunus: 98], the verse. The apparent meaning of the verse of as-Saffat is that they believed with true faith, and that Allah dealt with them as He deals with believers, and that is in His saying in as-Saffat: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more, and they believed, so We let them enjoy for a time﴾ [as-Saffat: 147–148], because the apparent unrestricted sense of His saying "and they believed" indicates that. And Allah knows best.

Among the nations that He explicitly stated He destroyed and made into tales is Saba', because He, may He be exalted, said concerning them: ﴿So We made them tales and scattered them completely﴾ [Saba': 19], the verse. His saying ﴿We made them tales﴾ means: reports and stories by which people are entertained and at which they marvel, as Ibn Duraid said in his Maqsura:

؎ Indeed a man is but a tale after him, so be a good tale for whoever is aware.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read this word tatran with tanwin: and this is the dialect of Kinanah, while the rest read it with the feminine alif maqsura without tanwin: and this is the dialect of most of the Arabs. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr softened the second hamzah in His saying jā'a ummatin, and the rest read it with full hamzah, as is well known. His saying ﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 44] is a verbal noun whose verb is not apparent: it is said bagida bu'dan (with two fathahs, baʿadan) and bu'dan (with a damma then sukun), i.e., he perished; so His saying bu'dan means total annihilation, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Unquestionably, away with Madyan as Thamud was taken away﴾ [Hud: 95]. The poet said:

؎ The benefit diminishes when the youth meets destruction; the words of the beloved are "do not be far," and indeed he has become far.

Sibawayh has said that bu'dan, suhqan and dafran (i.e., stench) are among the verbal nouns put in the accusative by verbs that are not apparent. End quote. And from this category is their saying: saqyan wa ra'yan, as in the saying of Nabigha Dhubyani: (p-334)

؎ I was informed of blessings, rebellious in separation: "Watering and pasturing for that reproachful, blaming one."

As for al-Ahadith in His saying ﴿and We made them ahadith﴾, concerning its singular there are two well-known views:

The first: that it is the plural of hadith, as you say: "these are the ahadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ," meaning by al-ahadith the plural of hadith. On this view it is among the irregular plurals that deviate from analogy, alluded to by Ibn Malik's saying in al-Khulasa:

؎ And [a plural] that departs from analogy: whatever contravenes the rule in the two categories [of breaking and diminutive].

By the two categories he means the broken plural and the diminutive, such as the broken plural of hadith as ahadith and of batil as abatil, and the diminutive of maghrib as mughayribān, and of 'ashiyyah as 'ushayshiyyah. Some of them said that it is a collective noun (ism jam') for hadith.

The second view: that al-ahadith is the plural of uhduthah, which is like udhhuka (a joke), ul'uba (a plaything), and u'juba (a wonder), with the first letter vowelled with a damma and the second with sukun: it is what people speak of for entertainment and wonder. In this meaning is the saying of Tawbah ibn al-Humayyir:

؎ Of the veiled, white-skinned women, whose companion loves, when a tale ends, that she repeat it.

This second view is more fitting here, since the plural in it runs according to analogy, and az-Zamakhshari affirmed it. And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾. In this noble verse, Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, commanded His messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, to eat of the good things, although at the time this verse was revealed, the only one of them present was our Prophet ﷺ. The good things are the lawful that is free of any doubt upon verification. And He commanded them to do righteous deeds. This indicates that eating what is lawful has an effect on righteous deeds, and that is so. What He commanded the messengers in this noble verse, He also commanded the believers of this Ummah, which is the best of nations, in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things that We have provided for you, and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]. The verse indicates that every messenger was commanded in his time to eat what is lawful and to do righteous deeds, and the effect of eating what is lawful on deeds is well known. In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O people, Allah is Pure and accepts only what is pure. Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51]" (p-335) And He said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things that We have provided for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]. Then he mentioned the man who travels for a long time, disheveled and covered in dust, whose food is unlawful, whose drink is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, and who is nourished with the unlawful, who raises his hands to the sky, saying, "O Lord, O Lord," but how could his supplication be answered? This clearly indicates that his supplication, which is among the greatest means of drawing near to Allah, did not benefit him, because he did not eat from what is lawful, nor drink from it, nor ride from it.

The author says: Indeed, we have clarified the meaning of these two verses, explained the parts of them that need explanation, and set out the verses that clarify their meaning in Surah al-Anbiya', in the discussion of His words: ﴿Indeed, this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves; all of them will return to Us.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 92–93]. We also explained the intended meaning of the word *ummah* (community), together with some Arabic evidence, and we gathered the various meanings of *ummah* in the Qur'an at the beginning of Surah Hud, in the discussion of His words: ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted community…﴾ [Hud: 8]. That suffices here, so there is no need to repeat it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So leave them in their confusion for a while﴾. Exalted and Majestic is He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to leave the disbelievers, that is, to leave them in their confusion (ghamrah) until a while, that is, a specific time with Allah. The apparent meaning is that it is the time of the end of their lifespans, by killing or death, and their journey to what they are destined for after death, of the punishment of the barzakh (intermediate state) and of the Hereafter. As for the view that the "while" mentioned refers to the time of their being killed or their death, al-Zamakhshari reported it from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, without any chain of transmission.

The statements of the people of knowledge on the meaning of "their confusion" (ghamrahum) all go back to one thing. Such is the saying of al-Kalbi regarding ghamrahum, that is, their ignorance; the saying of Ibn Bahr: "in their bewilderment"; the saying of Ibn Salam: "in their heedlessness"; and the saying of some of them: "in their misguidance." The meaning of all these statements is one, namely that He commanded him to leave them in what they are in of disbelief, misguidance, error, and sins. Al-Zamakhshari said: The ghamrah is the water that covers a person's full height, so it is used as a metaphor for what they are submerged in of their ignorance and blindness, or they are likened to players in the deep water for what they are upon of falsehood. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*Nights of idle play have carried me away, and I follow them, as if I were one striking about in a deep, playful flood.*

The form of command in His saying ﴿So leave them in their confusion﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 54] is for threat. It has been established in the science of principles (usul al-fiqh) in the discussion of command, and in the science of rhetoric (ma'ani) in the discussion of inshaʾ (non-declarative speech), that among the meanings that the form af'al (imperative) comes for is threat. This meaning indicated by this noble verse, the threatening of the disbelievers who denied our Prophet ﷺ, is made clear in other places,

- such as His saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by hope; they will soon know﴾ [al-Hijr: 3],
- and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers; give them time, a little﴾ [al-Tariq: 17],
- and His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire"﴾ [Ibrahim: 30],
- and His saying: ﴿Say: "Enjoy your disbelief for a little; indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire"﴾ [al-Zumar: 8].

We have clarified the verses indicating this meaning in Surat al-Hijr, in discussing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves and be diverted by hope﴾ [al-Hijr: 3], and we spoke there about the word "dhar-hum" (leave them).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they think that what We provide them with of wealth and children﴾ ﴿is Us hastening to them with good things? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ We have already explained the verses that clarify these two verses in Surah al-Kahf, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾. What this verse includes of ease in this upright (ḥanīfiyyah, the pure monotheistic way) that is tolerant and easy, which our Prophet (ﷺ) brought, we have already mentioned some of the verses that indicate it in Surat al-Ḥajj, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 78], so that suffices here instead of repeating it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with Us is a Book which speaks with truth, and they will not be wronged﴾. The correct view is that the intended meaning of this Book is the Book of deeds, in which Allah records them, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿This is Our Record; it speaks against you with truth. Indeed, We used to have transcribed what you were doing﴾ [al-Jāthiyah: 29]. We have already presented the verses clarifying this meaning in Surat al-Kahf, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], and in Surat al-Isrā' in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾ [al-Isrā': 13].

The apparent meaning of the Book's speaking with truth is that everything written in it is true. Whoever reads what is written in it, it is as if it speaks to him, in its recitation, only with truth. The Arabs sometimes apply the name of speech to writing (al-khaṭṭ), as it is related from ʿĀʾishah that she said: "What is between the two covers of the muṣḥaf is the speech of Allah." And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

﴿حَتّى إذا أخَذْنا مُتْرَفِيهِمْ بِالعَذابِ إذا هم يَجْأرُونَ﴾ ﴿لا تَجْأرُوا اليَوْمَ إنَّكم مِنّا لا تُنْصَرُونَ﴾ His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out for help.﴾ ﴿Do not cry out for help today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us.﴾ Here "until" (ḥattā) in this verse is the point after which the speech begins. The speech is the conditional clause ("when We seize..."). The punishment with which their Lord seized them has been said to be the punishment of the Day of Badr, by killing and capture. It has also been said to be the hunger and severe famine that afflicted them when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked against them, saying: "O Allah, press down Your foot upon Mudar. O Allah, make it upon them as years of famine like the years of Yusuf." So they were afflicted, because of his ﷺ supplication, with severe hunger, a painful punishment. The most evident of these views to me is that He seized them with punishment on the Day of Resurrection. Allah, Exalted, has clarified in these two verses that He seized their affluent ones with punishment. The affluent (mutrafūn) are the people of blessing and ease in the worldly abode. This meaning is indicated by His saying: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little. Indeed, with Us are shackles and a blazing Fire, and food that chokes, and a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11–13]. So His saying "possessors of luxury" means the affluent of the world, and He made clear that He would punish them after the threat, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles and a blazing Fire﴾ and so on.

As for His saying "yajʾarūn": al-juʾār (crying out, a loud cry seeking help) is shouting with a plea for rescue. The Arabs say: "jaʾara al-thawr yajʾaru" (the bull bellowed), meaning it cried out. So al-juʾār is like al-khuwār (the lowing). In some readings there is: ﴿a calf, a body that had a lowing (juʾār)﴾ [al-A'raf: 148; Ta-Ha: 88], with the letter jīm and hamza, meaning khuwār (lowing). And "jaʾara al-rajul ilā Allāh" means he humbled himself in supplication.

The meaning of the noble verse is: the affluent among the disbelievers in the world, when Allah seizes them with punishment on the Day of Resurrection, will cry out, shouting for help, seeking deliverance from what they are in. Their outcry and their pleading, indicated here, is mentioned in other verses, such as His saying, Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve, for them is the Fire of Hell; it will not be decreed upon them so that they die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ungrateful one.﴾ ﴿And they will cry out therein: "Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteousness other than what we used to do."﴾ [Fatir: 36–37]. So His saying "yaṣṭarikhūn" (they cry out) is from the form "yaftaʿilūn" from al-ṣurākh (shouting), pleading for rescue, wanting to get out of what they are in, as is evident from His saying about them: ﴿"Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteousness other than what we used to do."﴾ So this outcry mentioned in that verse, which is general to the affluent and others, is the same as the juʾār mentioned here about the affluent. Among the Arabs' use of juʾār for shouting and supplication for rescue is the saying of al-A'sha:

"He alternates, from the prayers of the King, sometimes prostration and sometimes juʾār."

The juʾār mentioned is the calling in His saying: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, and they called out, but it was no time for escape.﴾ [Sad: 3]; because their calling was a calling for rescue and seeking aid. And like His saying, Exalted: ﴿And they call out, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us."﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 77]; because a decree of death upon them is among the greatest things they seek, so they plead for death to escape the continuance of that severe punishment. May Allah protect us and our Muslim brothers from it. And like His saying, Exalted: ﴿And when they are thrown into a narrow place therein, bound together, they will call there for destruction.﴾ ﴿Do not call today for one destruction, but call for many destructions.﴾ [al-Furqan: 13–14]. That calling for destruction, which is the greatest ruin and perdition, is one of the kinds of their juʾār, and we seek refuge in Allah.

His saying, Exalted, in this verse: ﴿Do not cry out for help today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 65] indicates that if they seek rescue, they will not be rescued, and if they seek mercy, they will not be shown mercy. Allah, Exalted, has indicated this in His saying: ﴿And if they seek relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal, which scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place.﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 66:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My verses were recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels﴾, when He explained that the affluent among the disbelievers, when their Lord seizes them with the punishment, cry out, shout and call for help, and explained that they will not be helped, as we have clarified a moment ago, He explained the cause of that with His saying: "Indeed, My verses were recited to you", i.e., those with which I sent My messengers, "recited to you": they are read to you clearly and in detail. ﴿But you used to turn back on your heels﴾: you would retreat from them backward. The ʿaqib (heel) is the back part of the foot, and the nukus (turning back) is retreating from a matter. From it is His exalted saying: ﴿So when the two hosts saw each other, he turned back on his heels﴾ [al-Anfal: 48]. From it is also the saying of the poet:

They claimed that they were on the paths of salvation, but in truth they turned back on their heels.

This meaning that he mentioned here is indicated elsewhere, such as His exalted saying: ﴿They said: "Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice, and we have acknowledged our sins, so is there any way out?"﴾ ﴿That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved, but when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great﴾ [Ghafir: 11-12]. So their disbelief in the presence of Allah is the mention of Allah alone, from their turning back on their heels. He explained in another place that when His verses are recited to them, they do not limit themselves to turning back from them on their heels, but they nearly lash out at those who recite His verses to them, because of the intensity of their hatred for them. This is in His exalted saying: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear proofs, you recognize denial in the faces of those who disbelieve; they nearly assault those who recite Our verses to them﴾ [al-Hajj: 72]. (p-339) What we mentioned, that the punishment is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, is more apparent to us than the saying of one who said it is the Day of Badr or hunger, and than the saying of one who claimed that those who cry for help are those who were not killed on the Day of Badr and that their crying is on account of their brothers. All of that is contrary to the apparent meaning, even if whoever said it said it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 68:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not pondered over the Word?﴾ includes an exhortation to them to ponder over this Word, which is the Mighty Qur'an. For if they pondered over it with sincerity, they would know that it is the truth, that following it is obligatory, and that affirming the one who brought it is necessary. He has alluded to this meaning in other places, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not then ponder over the Qur'an? Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa': 82], and His saying: ﴿Do they not then ponder over the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24]. And His saying in this noble verse: ﴿Or has there come to them that which did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 68]. Al-Qurtubi said:

"They denied it and turned away from it. It was also said: 'Am' (أم) here means 'bal' (بل, rather): rather, there has come to them that which their forefathers had no knowledge of, and therefore they denied it and abandoned pondering over it."

Ibn 'Abbas said: It was also said that the meaning is: "Or has there come to them a security from the punishment, which did not come to their forefathers of old?" Abu Hayyan said in his tafsir of this verse: He first rebuked them for not benefiting from the Qur'an, then secondly by saying that what came to them had come to their forefathers of old, i.e., the sending of messengers is not an innovation nor something strange; rather, messengers were sent to the nations before them, and they knew this through mass transmission (tawatur), and through the salvation of those who believed and the annihilation of those who denied, and their forefathers were Isma'il and his descendants, to the end of his words. This interpretation has a valid aspect, and according to it the verse is like His saying: ﴿Say: I am not an innovation among the messengers﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 9], and similar verses.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have they not recognized their Messenger, so that they deny him?﴾ We have already presented the verses that clarify this verse in Surah Yunus, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I have remained among you a lifetime before it﴾ [Yunus: 16]. That suffices, so we do not repeat it here.

**The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 23, Verse 70**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they say, "There is madness in him"? Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ As for the *am* (or) mentioned in this verse, it is the one known to the grammarians as *am al-munqati'ah* (the disjunctive *am*). Its rule is that it is not preceded by a *hamzat taswiyah* (the equalizing interrogative hamza, which signals "whether... or"), as in ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], nor by a *hamzah mughniyah 'an lafdhah* (a hamza that stands in place of a verb), meaning a hamza that replaces a word. For example, as you say: "Is Zayd with you or 'Amr?" That is, which of them is with you? So the *am* preceded by one of the two hamzas mentioned is what they call *am al-muttasilah* (the connected *am*). The one not preceded by either of them is known as the disjunctive *am*, as it is here. The disjunctive *am* comes with three meanings.

The first: that it means *bal* (rather), signifying *al-idrab* (a shift of statement).

The second: that it means the hamza of interrogation expressing denial (*istifham al-inkar*).

The third: that it carries both meanings together, so it combines *al-idrab* and *al-inkar*. This last is the most common in its meaning, contrary to Ibn Malik in his *al-Khulasah*, in limiting it to the meaning of *bal* in his saying:

*And with disjunction, and with the meaning of "bal" and "wa-fat," if it is not among the things it is restricted by, it has been freed.*

By its being "freed" from what it is restricted by, he means that neither of the two hamzas mentioned precedes it. If one of the two hamzas precedes it, it is the connected *am*, as was mentioned just above. According to what we have mentioned, the meaning includes a shift away from what precedes it, a transitional shift (*idrab intiqali*), together with the meaning of the interrogation of denial. So the verse contains a denial addressed to the disbelievers in their claim that our Prophet ﷺ has *jinnah*, that is, madness. They mean that this truth which he has brought them is the raving of a madman. May Allah curse them! How stubbornly they reject the truth, and how thoroughly they disbelieve! Their claim against him, that he is mad, Allah has refuted here by His saying: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 70]. So the shift with *bal* is one of refutation (*idrab ibtali*).

The meaning is: He is not mad; rather, he is a noble messenger who has brought you the clear truth, supported by miracles, which every sensible person knows to be true. But you have been obstinate and have disbelieved, because of your extreme aversion to the truth. And what this noble verse negated, of their claim that he is mad, Allah has explicitly denied in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And your companion is not mad﴾ [al-Takwir: 22], and His saying: ﴿So by the grace of your Lord, you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾ [al-Tur: 29]. This madness that was attributed to the last of the prophets was also attributed to the first of them, as He, exalted is He, said in this noble surah concerning the people of Nuh (Noah) that they said about him: ﴿He is only a man with madness in him, so wait for him for a time﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 25]. In another place He has explained that Allah did not send a messenger except that his people said: "He is a sorcerer, or a madman," as if they had gathered and agreed upon this. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus did there not come to those before them any messenger except that they said, "A sorcerer or a madman." ﴾ ﴿Did they charge one another with it? Rather, they are a transgressing people﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52–53]. So He explained that the cause of their agreement on this was not that they had charged one another with it, because of the difference of their times and places. Rather, what gathered them upon this was the resemblance of some of them to others in transgression. This meaning has been clarified in Surah al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿Likewise said those before them, the like of their statement. Their hearts have become alike﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118]. So these verses indicate that the reason for the similarity of their statements to their messengers is the similarity of their hearts in disbelief, transgression, and aversion to the truth.

As for His saying: ﴿But most of them are averse to the truth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 70], He mentioned something similar in meaning in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have certainly brought you the truth, but most of you are averse to the truth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 78]. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, clear proofs, you recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve the denial﴾ [al-Hajj: 72]. That denial which you recognize in their faces is only because of their extreme aversion to the truth. Among the verses that make clear their aversion to the truth is that they refuse to hear it, and they use means that prevent them from hearing it, as He, exalted is He, said in the story of the first of the messengers whom He sent with His tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness) and the prohibition of associating partners with Him, who was Nuh: ﴿And indeed, whenever I called them, that You might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and were arrogantly proud, with great arrogance﴾ [Nuh: 7]. They only put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments out of fear that they would hear what their prophet Nuh, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, was saying to them of the truth and the call to it. And He, exalted is He, said concerning the nation of the last of the prophets ﷺ: ﴿And those who disbelieve said, "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it"﴾ [Fussilat: 26]. So you see some of them forbidding others from hearing it and ordering them to make noise during it, such as shouting and clapping that prevent hearing, because of their aversion to the truth and their attempt to overcome the truth with falsehood.

This noble verse raises a well-known question: that is, it may be said that His saying: ﴿But most of them are averse to the truth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 70] implies by the understanding of its opposite (*mafhum al-mukhalafah*) that a few of the disbelievers are not averse to the truth. This question also applies to the verse in Surah al-Zukhruf that we mentioned just above, namely His saying: ﴿But most of you are averse to the truth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 78].

The answer to this question is what some of the scholars have given: that a few of the disbelievers did not hate the truth, and the reason for their refraining from belief in Allah and His Messenger was not their aversion to the truth. Rather, the cause was pride and disdain of being rebuked by their people, and of their people saying that they had turned away (*sabau*) and abandoned the religion of their forefathers. Among the examples of one to whom this happened is Abu Talib, for he did not hate the truth that the Prophet ﷺ brought, and he used to support him in conveying his message, as we have already mentioned in his poetry, in his saying:

*Proclaim your command; there is no shame for you in it,*
*and give good tidings, and be pleased by it, and make it clear...*

(The verses continue, and he said in them:)

*Indeed I know that the religion of Muhammad*
*is among the best religions of mankind in religion.*

He also said about him ﷺ:

*They surely know that our son is not one who is accused of lying among us,*
*nor does he stray with the speech of falsehoods.*

Abu Talib has made clear in his poetry that the reason preventing him from embracing Islam was not aversion to the truth, but rather pride and fear of the blame of his people or their reviling him, as in his saying:

*Had it not been for blame, or fear of insult,*
*you would have found me generous, certainly, in that.*

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 71:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted﴾. The scholars differed concerning what is meant by "the truth" (al-haqq) in this verse. Some of them said: "The truth" is Allah, may He be exalted. It is well known that al-Haqq is among His Most Beautiful Names, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will know that Allah is the Manifest Truth﴾ [An-Nur: 25], and His saying: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ [Al-Hajj: 6]. That the intended meaning of "the truth" in the verse is Allah was attributed by al-Qurtubi to the majority, and among those who held this view are Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, Abu Salih, as-Suddi, and it is narrated from Qatadah, and others.

According to this view, the meaning is: if Allah had granted them what they wished in legislating what they wanted to legislate, and in sending whomever they proposed to send, by making the matter of legislation and the sending of messengers and the like follow their corrupt desires, then the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would be corrupted. This is because their corrupt desires and their false appetites cannot be the foundation on which the heavens and the earth stand, and that is due to the corruption of their desires and their divergence. Corrupt and divergent desires cannot be the basis for the order of the heavens, the earth, and whoever is in them. Rather, if they were the ones followed, everything would be ruined.

Among the verses indicating that their desires are not fit to be followed is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man from the two cities, a great one?"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 31]. For if the Qur'an had been sent down upon one of the two men mentioned, who was an unbeliever worshipping idols, there would be no greater corruption than that. Allah has refuted them with His saying: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 32] to the end of the verse. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Say, "If you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, then you would withhold them, fearing expenditure. And mankind is ever stingy."﴾ [Al-Isra': 100]. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Or do they have a share of the kingdom? For then they would not give the people even a speck.﴾ [An-Nisa': 53]. Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "In all of this is a demonstration of the helplessness of the servants, the divergence of their opinions and desires, and that He, may He be exalted, is the Perfect in all His attributes, His sayings, His actions, His legislation, His decree, and His management of His creation, glorified and exalted be He far above that."

(p-343) And among the things that clarify that if the Truth followed corrupt and divergent desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would be corrupted, is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 22], ﴿Glorified is Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾.

The second view: that the intended meaning of "the truth" in the verse is the truth which is the opposite of falsehood, mentioned in the verse before it: ﴿And most of them are averse to the truth﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 70]. This last view was chosen by Ibn 'Atiyyah, who rejected the first.

According to this view, the meaning is: if it were assumed that the truth followed their desires, which are associating partners with Allah, claiming children and rivals for Him, and the like, then everything would be corrupted. This is because, under this assumption, the truth itself would become the greatest falsehood, and the order of the heavens and the earth cannot stand upon something that is the greatest falsehood. The soundness of the order of this world is only possible by the power and will of a God who is the Truth, alone in legislating, commanding and forbidding, as is not hidden from any rational person. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they, from their reminder, are turning away﴾. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of "reminder" (dhikr) in the verse. Some of them said: their "reminder" is their pride and their honour, because the revelation of this Book upon a man from among them contains for them the greatest pride and honour. On this view, the verse is like His saying: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 44], with dhikr interpreted as pride and honour. Others said: the "reminder" in the verse is admonition and exhortation, and on this view the verse is like His saying: ﴿That which We recite to you of the signs and the wise reminder﴾ [Al 'Imran: 58]. Others said: the "reminder" is what they used to wish for, in His saying: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been sincere servants of Allah﴾ [As-Saffat: 168-169]. On this view, the verse is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that if a warner came to them, they would be better guided than any of the nations﴾ [Fatir: 42]. On this view, His saying: ﴿But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾ [Fatir: 42], to the end of the verse, is like His saying here: ﴿so they, from their reminder, are turning away﴾, and like His saying: ﴿Or you should say, "If the Book had been revealed to us, we would have been better guided than they"﴾ [Al-An'am: 157]. The verses of this kind, according to the last view, are numerous. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do you ask them for any payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾ (p-344) What is meant by al-kharj and al-kharaj here is: wage and reward.

The meaning is: you do not ask them, for what you have conveyed to them of the message, which comprises the good of both this world and the Hereafter, any wage or recompense. The root sense of al-kharj and al-kharaj is what one pays out to every worker in return for his wage, or for a stipend (ja'l). This noble verse includes that he, peace and blessings be upon him, does not ask them for any wage in return for conveying the message.

We have already explained the Qur'anic verses indicating that the messengers do not take payment for conveying the message in Surah Hud, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted, concerning Noah: ﴿And O my people, I do not ask you for any wealth; my reward is only from Allah﴾ up to the end of the verse [Hud: 29]. We also explained the way of reconciling those verses with the verse: ﴿Say, I do not ask you for any reward for it, except affection among relatives﴾ [al-Shura: 23]. There we also explained the ruling on taking payment for teaching the Qur'an and other things, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Ibn 'Amir read these two words as: khar-jan fa-kharju rabbika, with the ra' vowelless in both, and the alif omitted in both. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: kharajan fa-kharaju rabbika, with a fatha on the ra' followed by an alif in both. The rest read: khar-jan fa-kharaju rabbika, with the ra' vowelless and the alif omitted in the first, and with a fatha on the ra' and the alif present in the second.

The sound position is that the meanings of al-kharj and al-kharaj are one and the same, and that they are two eloquent dialects and two canonical recitations, contrary to those who claim that there is a difference between their meanings, asserting that al-kharj is what you give voluntarily, and al-kharaj is what it is obligatory for you to pay. The meaning of the verse does not support this distinction, as you see, and Allah knows best.

The form of comparative in His saying: ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 72] is in view of the fact that some created beings provide for others, as in His saying: ﴿and provide for them therein and clothe them﴾ [al-Nisa': 5], and His saying: ﴿and upon the father of the child is their provision and their clothing﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Baqarah: 233]. There is no doubt that the excellence of Allah's provision to His creation over the provision of some of His creatures to others is like the excellence of His essence and all His attributes over the essences and attributes of His creatures.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path﴾. We have already presented the clarifying verses explaining the meaning of this verse in Surah al-Hajj, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And invite to your Lord; indeed, you are upon guidance, straight﴾ [al-Hajj: 67], so it suffices from repeating it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ In this noble verse, He, may He be glorified and exalted, mentions that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, because of their denial of resurrection and recompense, are deviating from the path (al-sirat). What is meant by the path from which they deviate is the straight path (al-sirat al-mustaqim) (p-345) that leads to Paradise, mentioned in His saying before it: ﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 73] Whoever deviates from this straight path enters the Fire without doubt.

The verses indicating this are many, such as His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-Rum: ﴿And as for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, they will be brought into the punishment.﴾ [al-Rum: 16] The meaning of His saying "lanakibun" (deviating) is: swerving away from it, turning aside, not travelling along it. This is a well-known meaning in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of Nusayb:

"O my two companions from Ka'b, did you two guide me to Zaynab? May Ka'b never lose you two.
From today, visiting her, for our mounts on the morrow are turning away from her and from her people."

The plural of nakibah (turning away), "anha," meaning: swerving away from her and distancing from her, and from her people.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 75:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if We had mercy upon them and removed what afflicts them of adversity, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. We have already clarified the verses that explain what this verse indicates, namely that He, exalted is He, knows the non-existent thing that, in His knowledge, He has determined would not exist, [knowing] what it would be if it did exist. This was discussed in surah al-An'am in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars﴾ [al-An'am: 28], so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here. As for His saying in this verse: ﴿they would persist in their transgression﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 75], al-lajaj (obstinate persistence) here means continuing in disbelief and error. At-tughyan (transgression) means exceeding the limit, and it refers to their disbelief in Allah and their attributing to Him children and partners. As for His saying: ya'mahun (wandering blindly), it means wandering about, bewildered, not distinguishing truth from falsehood. Some scholars of knowledge said: al-'amah (blindness) is blindness of the heart. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they entreat Him.﴾ In this noble verse, He mentions that He seized the disbelievers with punishment. The apparent meaning here is worldly punishment, such as hunger, drought, calamities, illnesses, and hardships. ﴿They did not humble themselves before their Lord﴾ means they did not submit to Him and were not humbled. ﴿Nor did they entreat﴾ means they did not beseech Him with supplication, humbly imploring Him, so that He would remove that punishment from them. This was due to the severe hardness of their hearts and their remoteness from taking admonition, even though they were deserving of the punishment of Allah being inflicted upon them because of what they had committed. This meaning that he mentioned here is clarified in other places, such as His saying in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And We indeed sent to nations before you, then We seized them with adversity and hardship, so that they might humble themselves.﴾ ﴿Why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts were hardened, and Satan made attractive to them what they used to do.﴾ [al-An'am: 42-43]. And His saying in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿And We did not send a prophet to any town without seizing its people with adversity and hardship, so that they might entreat.﴾ ﴿Then We replaced the bad with good until they multiplied, and said, "Adversity and ease had touched our forefathers," so We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive.﴾ [al-A'raf: 94-95], and other verses besides these.

[p-346]

Allah says: ﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful.﴾ I have already mentioned the verses that clarify the meaning of this verse in Surat an-Nahl, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts that you may be grateful﴾ [an-Nahl 16:78]. There I also explained the reason why "hearing" is in the singular while "sight" and "hearts" are in the plural, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who multiplied you in the earth, and to Him you will be gathered﴾. "Dhara'akum" (multiplied you) means: He created you. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], to the end of the verse. His saying "in the earth" means: He created you and dispersed you in the earth through procreation, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And from the two of them He spread forth many men and women﴾ [an-Nisa': 1], to the end of the verse. And He said: ﴿Then, when you are human beings, you disperse [throughout the earth]﴾ [ar-Rum: 20]. His saying: ﴿And to Him you will be gathered﴾ means: to Him alone you will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, alive after being raised, for recompense and reckoning.

What this verse includes, that He created them, dispersed them in the earth, and that He will gather them to Himself on the Day of Resurrection, has the same meaning in many verses. Such as His saying at the beginning of this surah: ﴿And We did certainly create man from an extract of clay﴾, up to His saying: ﴿Then indeed, after that, you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12–16]. He, majestic and exalted, also mentioned these two verses in Surah al-Mulk in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "It is He who produced you and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful."﴾ ﴿Say, "It is He who multiplied you in the earth, and to Him you will be gathered."﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ [al-Mulk: 23–25]. And the verses on this meaning are many.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 80:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who gives life and causes death﴾. We have already presented the verses indicating the two deaths and the two lives, and that this is among the greatest incentives to belief in Him, may He be glorified and exalted, in Surat al-Hajj in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And it is He who gave you life, then causes you to die, then gives you life again﴾ [al-Hajj: 66], and in Surat al-Baqarah in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. That suffices and makes its repetition here unnecessary.

* *

(p-347) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And His is the alternation of the night and the day. Will you not then reason?﴾ In this noble verse, He, may He be glorified and exalted, has made clear that His is the alternation of the night and the day, meaning that He is the one who does this, and He is the One who takes away the night and brings the day, then takes away the day and brings the night. The alternation of the night and the day is among His greatest signs indicating the perfection of His power, and among His greatest favours upon His creation, as He explained both matters in Surat al-Qasas in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you light? Will you not then listen?" Say: "Have you considered, if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than Allah could bring you a night in which you rest? Will you not then see?" And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ [al-Qasas: 71–73], meaning: that you may rest at night and seek your livelihood by day. The verses indicating the alternation of the night and the day are among the greatest signs indicating the greatness of Allah and His being deserving of worship alone, and they are very numerous, such as:

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day﴾ [Fussilat: 37].

• And His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day, and they are then in darkness﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37].

• And His saying: ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54].

• And His saying: ﴿Nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He subjected for you the night and the day﴾ [Ibrahim: 33].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day, and what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, are signs for a people who fear Allah﴾ [Yunus: 6].

Verses like these are very numerous. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ means: will you perceive with your intellects that He who brings into being the hearing, the sight and the hearts, ﴿scattered you throughout the earth, and to Him you will be gathered﴾, and ﴿it is He who gives life and causes death﴾, and who alternates the night and the day, is the true God, worshipped alone, may He be glorified and exalted, whom none may rightly be equated with, far exalted is He above that, to a great degree.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 81:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, they said the like of what the ancients said.﴾ ﴿They said: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised up?"﴾ The word "bal" (nay, rather) here is for a transitional turning away (al-id'rab al-intiqali).

The meaning: the disbelievers who denied our Prophet (ﷺ) said the like of what the nations before them said, namely denying the Resurrection. This is because the interrogative in His saying "shall we indeed be raised up?" is a denial from them of the Resurrection. The verses indicating their denial of the Resurrection are numerous:

• such as His saying, Exalted is He, about them: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78]

• and His saying about them: ﴿And we shall not be resurrected﴾ [al-An'am: 29] (p-348) ﴿And we shall not be raised up﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 35]

• and His saying about them: ﴿When we are bones, decayed, [they say]: "That, then, would be a losing return."﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 11-12]. The verses of this kind concerning their denial of the Resurrection are numerous. We have explained, in surah al-Baqarah, in the commentary on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you﴾ (the verse) [al-Baqarah: 21], and at the beginning of surah an-Nahl, and elsewhere, the verses indicating resurrection after death, and we cited many of them.

• such as His saying: ﴿Say: "He will give them life who brought them into being the first time"﴾ (the verse) [Ya-Sin: 79],

• and His saying: ﴿And it is He who begins creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [ar-Rum: 27],

• and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust﴾ (the verses) [al-Hajj: 5]. We have set out four Qur'anic proofs indicating resurrection after death, and we have multiplied the mention of the verses indicating this, which makes further lengthy discussion here unnecessary.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, in this verse, "shall we when we are dead": Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read with the interrogative in "a-idha mitna" and dropped the interrogative hamza in "a-inna lamab'uthun," reading "inna lamab'uthun" in the declarative form, relying on the first interrogative to indicate the omitted second interrogative. Ibn 'Amir read it the reverse way: he dropped the interrogative hamza from "a-idha," reading "idha" without interrogative, and kept the interrogative hamza in His saying "a-inna lamab'uthun," since the second interrogative that is affirmed in Ibn 'Amir's reading indicates the omitted first interrogative. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah read with the interrogative in both: "a-idha mitna wa-kunna turaban wa-'idaman a-inna lamab'uthun." They follow their principles regarding the two hamzas: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr soften (tashil) the second, and the rest pronounce it fully (tahqiq). Qalun, Abu 'Amr and Hisham, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, insert an alif between the two hamzas, and the rest read with shortening (qasr) without the alif. Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read "mitna" with a kasra on the mim, and the rest with a damma on the mim. We have already discussed in surah Maryam, in the commentary on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿She said: "Would that I had died before this"﴾ (the verse) [Maryam: 23], the reason for the kasra on the mim in attributing the verb "mata" (to die) to the ta' of the subject. We explained that this is hidden from many students of knowledge, and we clarified the sense of "ghayah" (an extremity or purpose) along with some Arabic evidence, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed we have been promised this, we and our fathers before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾

In this noble verse, He - majestic and exalted - mentions that the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection said that they had been promised the resurrection, and their fathers before them had been promised it too. The apparent meaning is that they mean their forefathers to whom the messengers came and informed them that they would be raised after death for reckoning and recompense. They said that the resurrection they had been promised, they and their fathers, is a lie with no reality to it, and that it is nothing but "asatir al-awwalin" (fables of the ancients), that is, what they inscribed and wrote of falsehoods and trivialities. "Asatir" is the plural of "ustura" (fable), and it was said that it is the plural of "usṭara." This statement of theirs about denying the resurrection is mentioned similarly in Surah an-Naml, in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "When we and our fathers have become dust, will we really be brought out?" We have certainly been promised this, we and our fathers before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾ [An-Naml: 67-68]. Then He, exalted is He, established the proof for the resurrection that they denied in this verse, by His saying: ﴿Say, "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?"﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 84-89]; because the One to whom the earth and whoever is in it belongs, and who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne, and in whose hand is the dominion of everything, ﴿and He protects, but none can be protected against Him﴾, there is no doubt that He is able to resurrect people after death, as we have clarified earlier, the Qur'anic decisive proofs indicating that.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 84:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs the earth and whatever is in it, if you know?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say: "Will you not then remember?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ ﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion (malakūt) of all things, and He protects, and none can be protected against Him, if you know?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say: "How then are you deluded?"﴾ We have already presented what these noble verses indicate of His perfection, His majesty, and the attributes of His lordship, which necessitate sincerity of worship to Him alone, in surah Yunus in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They invent﴾, and ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who controls hearing and sight? And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living? And who arranges the affair?" They will say, "Allah." So say, "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ [Yunus: 31]. And in surah al-Isra' in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9]. We have clarified that the evidence of His oneness in lordship indicates His oneness in worship, and we have mentioned many Qur'anic verses that indicate this, with clarification, so that suffices in place of repeating it here.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿in whose hand is the dominion (malakūt) of all things﴾: al-malakūt is on the pattern of fa‘lūt, derived from al-mulk, meaning: in whose hand is the sovereignty of all things, that is, He who is the owner of all things, whatever they may be. Some scholars have said: the addition of the waw and the ta' in words such as al-malakūt, al-rahamūt, and al-rahabūt, with the meanings of sovereignty, mercy, and fear, indicates intensification (mubālagha) in that meaning. And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿and He protects, and none can be protected against Him﴾, meaning: He grants protection to whom He wills against whom He wills, and no one can grant protection from Him to anyone whom He wills to destroy or punish, because He alone is the One able over all things. ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾ [al-An'am: 18]. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I see you have begun to wrong those whom we have protected,
and the wronging of one who gives protection is the humiliation of the protector."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾, meaning: how are you deceived and turned away from the oneness of your Lord and from obeying Him, despite the manifestation of His decisive proofs and His clear evidences? It has also been said: ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾ means: how is it imagined to you that you associate with Him what neither harms nor benefits and cannot avail you anything, based on the premise that sihr (magic) is takhyīl (the creation of illusion).

We have already presented the discussion of magic comprehensively in surah Ta-Ha, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the magician does not succeed wherever he goes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69]. The apparent meaning of tus'harūn here is: you are deceived by false doubts, so that your intellects are led away from the truth, just as is done to the one who is bewitched. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying: ﴿a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn﴾ (Will you not then remember?), it was recited by Ḥafṣ from ‘Āṣim, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisā'ī with the dhāl lightened by omitting one of the two tā's, while the rest read it with the dhāl doubled (tashdīd) by assimilating one of the two tā's into the dhāl.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will say, "To Allah"﴾, it occurs three times in these verses. The first is: ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say: "Will you not then remember?"﴾. All of the seven readers agreed on reciting this one with the lām of jarr (the preposition lām) attached to the word Allah, because it is the answer to the question introduced by the lām of jarr, which is His saying: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs the earth and whatever is in it?"﴾. So the answer to "To whom belongs the earth?" is that you say: "To Allah" (li-Llāh). As for the second, which is: ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾, and the third, which is His saying: ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say: "How then are you deluded?"﴾, Abū ‘Amr recited both of them by omitting the lām of jarr and raising the hā' of the word Allah (Allāhu).

The meaning according to the reading of Abū ‘Amr mentioned above is clear and free of difficulty, because the apparent answer to "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?" is that you say: "Allah," in the nominative, meaning: the Lord of what has been mentioned is Allah. Likewise, the answer to His saying: ﴿In whose hand is the dominion of all things﴾, and so on, apparently is also that it be said: "Allah" in the nominative, meaning: He in whose hand is the dominion of all things. So Abū ‘Amr's reading follows the apparent meaning, which has no difficulty. The other readers of the seven read the two mentioned words with the preposition of jarr and the hā' of the word Allah in the genitive, as in the first.

In this reading, which is the reading of the majority, there is a well-known question: what is the reason for using the lām of jarr, given that the question does not require an answer with it? For the saying "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?" apparently requires the answer: "Their Lord is Allah," and in that case the reason for using the lām of jarr becomes problematic. The answer to this question is well known and clear, because His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is the Lord of the heavens﴾, and so on, and His saying: ﴿In whose hand is the dominion of all things﴾, contain the meaning: who is the owner of the heavens, the earth, the Throne, and all things. So it is appropriate to answer with "To Allah," meaning: all of that belongs to Allah. A parallel from the speech of the Arabs is the saying of the poet:

"When it is asked, 'Who is the lord of the villages (al-mazālif) and the towns, and the lord of the thoroughbred horses?' I say: 'To Khālid.'"

Because His saying: "Who is the lord of the villages" contains the meaning "who is the owner of them," the answer with the lām was appropriate: that is, they belong to Khālid. Al-mazālif is the plural of mazlafa, like marḥala. In al-Qāmūs he said: it is every village that lies between the open desert and the cultivated land, and its plural is mazālif.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 91:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, nor has there been with Him any god. [If there were], then each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others. Exalted is Allah above what they describe.﴾ In this noble verse, Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, clarifies three matters:

The first: that He has not taken a son, glorified and exalted is He above that by a great exaltation.

The second: that there is no other god with Him, glorified and exalted is He above that by a great exaltation.

The third: that He has established the proof for the impossibility of there being multiple gods, by His saying: ﴿If there were [other] gods with Him, then each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others.﴾

As for their claim that He has children, we have already clarified the verses indicating the great enormity of their slander in this matter and the clear falsehood of their claim, and Allah refuted them on this in several places. We explained in Surah An-Nahl, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters—glory be to Him—and for themselves what they desire﴾ and ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female...﴾ [An-Nahl: 57–58], the verse. We mentioned a portion of it at the beginning of Al-Kahf, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ [Al-Kahf: 4], and in places other than what was mentioned, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

As for His being singled out in divinity together with the establishment of the proof for that, we have clarified it and mentioned the verses that indicate it in Surah Bani Isra'il, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Say, "If there were gods with Him as they say, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne."﴾ [Al-Isra': 42]. We did not address what the theologians call the "proof of mutual exclusion" (dalil al-tamanu') because of the abundance of objections raised against the people of kalam (scholastic theology) concerning it; rather, we clarified the verses by the Qur'an through the Qur'anic method of inference from them, so that sufficed and there is no need to repeat it here.

(p-352) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised,﴾ ﴿My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people.﴾ In these two noble verses, Allah, exalted and majestic is He, commanded His Prophet to say: "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised," that is, if You should show me the punishment You threaten them with, by sending it down upon them while I am present, witnessing and seeing its descent upon them. ﴿Do not place me among the wrongdoing people,﴾ that is, do not place me among the totality of the punished wrongdoers; rather, remove me from among them and save me from their punishment. Allah, exalted, has explained in other places that the punishment does not descend upon them while he (the Prophet) is among them, and this is in His saying, exalted: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]. Here He has explained that He is able to show him the punishment He promised them, in His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 95]. And He explained in Surat al-Zukhruf that if He takes him away before their punishment, then He will certainly punish them and take vengeance upon them, and that if He punishes them while he is present, then He is Almighty over them. This is in His saying, exalted: ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed, We will take vengeance upon them, or We show you that which We have promised them, indeed, We are Omnipotent over them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 41-42].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 96:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Repel evil with that which is better; We are most knowing of what they describe.﴾ ﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils.﴾ ﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me."﴾ What these three verses contain is what should be the manner of dealing with the devils of mankind and the devils of the jinn. We have already presented, with clarification, the verses indicating this at the end of Surat al-A'raf, in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Take what is easy, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ ﴿And if an evil whisper from Satan reaches you, seek refuge in Allah﴾ and the verse [al-A'raf: 199-200]. His saying in this verse, "with that which is better," means: with the quality which is the best of qualities. "As-sayyi'ah" (evil) is the object of "idfa'" (repel). The morphological pattern of "sayyi'ah" is fay'alah; its original form was "sayyi'uwah," and its root letters are the sin, the waw and the hamzah. The unvowelled ya' was inserted between the fa' and the 'ayn, so it became obligatory to change the waw which is the 'ayn of the word into a ya', and to assimilate the ya' of the fay'alah which is added to it, according to the morphological rule referred to by Ibn Malik's saying in the Khulasah:

"If a waw preceded by a sukun is joined to a ya', and it is free from an 'arud (prosodic) element, then change the waw into a ya' and assimilate it, but the anomalous word mu'ta (for mu'twa) departs from what has been written."

as we have mentioned repeatedly.

And "as-sayyi'ah" in the language means: a quality from the qualities of evil. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We are most knowing of what they describe﴾ means: of what their tongues describe of lies in their denial of you, and their claiming of children and partners for Allah. We have already mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah that the gentleness and forgiveness required in the verses of the Qur'an after the revelation of fighting apply only with respect to the believers, not the disbelievers, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54], and we explained the verses indicating that, such as His saying about the Prophet ﷺ and his companions: ﴿hard against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29];

• and His saying: ﴿and lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88];

• and His saying: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73], up to the end of what preceded.

His saying in this verse: ﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils. And I seek refuge﴾: "hamazat" is the plural of "hamzah," which is one instance of the verb "hamz." In the language, hamz means prodding and pushing. "Hamazat al-shayatin" are their prods to the children of Adam to urge and incite them toward sins, as we clarified the discussion of it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement﴾ [Maryam: 83].

• And like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is to him a companion﴾ ﴿And indeed, they bar them from the way﴾ and the verse [al-Zukhruf: 36-37].

The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me﴾ is: I seek refuge in You lest Satan be present with me in any of my affairs, whatever it may be, whether that is at the time of reciting the Qur'an, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl: 98], or at the presence of death, or other than that, from all matters at all times. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: "My Lord, send me back, ﴾ ﴿that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind." No! ﴾ In my view, the apparent meaning is that "ḥattā" (until) in this verse is the one after which speech begins, and it is called the particle of beginning (ḥarf ibtidāʾ), as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said. This differs from al-Zamakhsharī, who said it is the limit (ghāya) of His saying: ﴿We know best what they describe﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 96], and from Abū Ḥayyān, who said that the apparent view for him is that before it there is an omitted clause, which is its limit, indicated by what precedes it. He estimated the omitted clause, as stated, as: "Then I would not be like the disbelievers whom the devils prod and who are present with them," ﴿until, when death comes to one of them, he says: "My Lord, send me back."﴾ A parallel to the omission of this clause is the poet al-Farazdaq's verse:

"How strange! Even Kulayb reviles me, as though his father were Nahshal or Mujāshiʿ."

He said: the meaning is "People revile me, even Kulayb," so what follows "ḥattā" indicates the omitted clause. In the verse, what precedes it indicates it. This ends the purpose of Abū Ḥayyān's words, and it does not appear to me to be entirely clear.
