Rather, the more apparent view to me is what I have put forward, which is the view of Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and what this noble verse contains: that the disbeliever and the one who neglected good deeds, when death comes to either of them, both seek to return to life so that they may do the righteous deed that will admit them to Paradise and make up for what they previously committed of disbelief and neglect. They are not granted this, as indicated by the particle of rebuke and repulsion, which is "kallā" (No!). It is clarified in other places, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And spend of what We have provided you before death comes to one of you, and he says: "My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term, so I would give charity and be among the righteous." ﴾ ﴿But Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come.﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10–11], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And warn the people of the Day when the punishment will come to them, and those who did wrong will say: "Our Lord, delay us to a near term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers." Had you not sworn before that you would have no decline?﴾ [Ibrahim: 44], and other verses. Just as they seek to return at the presence of death in order to set right their deeds, so they seek that on the Day of Resurrection, and it is known that they will not be answered in that.

Among the verses that indicate this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day its interpretation comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord came with the truth. Do we have any intercessors to intercede for us, or could we be returned so that we might do other than what we used to do?"﴾ [al-Araf: 53]. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If only you could see when the criminals bow their heads before their Lord: "Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so send us back and we will do righteousness; indeed we are certain."﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12]. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire and say: "Oh, if only we could be returned and not deny the signs of our Lord and be among the believers!" ﴾ ﴿But there has appeared to them what they had been concealing before. And even if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars.﴾ [al-Anʿam: 27–28]. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, saying: "Is there any way of return?"﴾ [al-Shura: 44]. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They say: "Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice, and we have confessed our sins, so is there any way out?"﴾ [Ghafir: 11]. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will cry out therein: "Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteousness other than what we used to do." Did We not give you lives long enough for whoever would remember to remember? And the warner came to you. So taste, for the wrongdoers have no helper.﴾ [Fatir: 37]. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified and there is no escape, and they are seized from a near place. ﴾ ﴿And they will say, "We believe in it." But how can they reach it from a far place? ﴾ ﴿And they had disbelieved in it before﴾ and so on [Saba: 51–53]. These verses that we have mentioned, and their like in the Qurʾan, contain that they ask for return and are not answered at the presence of death, on the Day of Resurrection, at the time of their being presented before Allah, the Exalted, and at the time of their being presented before the Fire.

In this noble verse there is a well-known question: what is the reason for the plural form in His saying ﴿My Lord, send me back (irjiʿūnī)﴾, when He did not say "send me back" (irjiʿnī) in the singular?

We have clarified the answer to this in our book "Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb" (Removing the Illusion of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), and we explained that it is answered in three ways:

The first, which is the most apparent of them: the plural form in "irjiʿūnī" is for the glorification of the one addressed, and that regretful one who asks for return shows at that time the glorification of his Lord. A parallel to this in the speech of the Arabs is the poet Ḥassān ibn Thābit's, or another's, saying:

"Oh, have mercy on me, God of Muḥammad! If I am not worthy, You are worthy of it."

And another's saying, addressing a woman:

"If you wish, I will forbid women other than you, and if you wish, I will not taste cool water or sleep."

Al-Nuqākh is cold water, and al-Bard is sleep; it was said it is the opposite of heat, but the first is more apparent.

The second way: His saying "My Lord" is an appeal to Him, may He be exalted, and His saying "send me back (irjiʿūnī)" is an address to the angels. This way is supported by what Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to ʿĀʾisha: "When the believer sees the angels, they say: 'We will return you to the abode of the world.' He says: 'To the abode of worries and sorrows?' He says: 'Rather, send me forward to Allah.' As for the disbeliever, they say to him: 'We will return you,' and he says: 'My Lord, send me back (irjiʿūnī).'"

The third way: it is the saying of al-Māzinī, that he used the plural pronoun to indicate repetition, as if he had said: "My Lord, send me back, send me back, send me back." The distance of this view is not hidden, as you see, and Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿That I may do righteous deeds﴾. The apparent view is that "laʿalla" here is for causation, meaning: "send me back so that I may do righteous deeds." It was said that it expresses hope and expectation, because he is not certain that if he is returned to the world he will do righteous deeds. The first is more apparent. The righteous deed includes all deeds, from the two testimonies, and the pilgrimage he had neglected, and the prayers, and zakat, and the like. Allah knows best. His saying "kallā" (No!) is a word of rebuke, which indicates that the return he sought will not be granted to him, as is clear.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in "Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb":

(p. 350) In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah Qad Aflaha al-Muʾminun (Surah 23).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He says: "My Lord, send me back (irjiʿūnī)."﴾

What comes to mind about the return of the pronoun to the Lord is not hidden, since the pronoun is in the plural form while the Lord, may He be majestic and exalted, is one.

The answer is in three ways:

The first, which is the most apparent of them: the plural form is for the glorification of the one addressed, who is Allah, meaning, as in the poet's saying:

"Oh, have mercy on me, God of Muḥammad! If I am not worthy, You are worthy of it."

And another's saying:

"If you wish, I will forbid women other than you, and if you wish, I will not taste cool water or sleep."

The second way: His saying "My Lord" is an appeal to Him, may He be exalted, and His saying "send me back (irjiʿūnī)" is an address to the angels. This way is supported by what Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the believer sees the angels, they say: 'Shall we return you to the abode of the world?' He says: 'To the abode of worries and sorrows?' He says: 'Rather, send me forward to Allah.' As for the disbelievers, they say to him: 'We will return you,' and he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back.﴾"

The third way: it is the saying of al-Māzinī, that he used the plural pronoun to indicate repetition, as if he had said: "My Lord, send me back, send me back." In my view, this saying is somewhat distant, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 101:

(p-356) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask one another.﴾ In this noble verse there are two well-known questions which require a clarifying answer that resolves the difficulty.

The first question: He, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse that when the Trumpet is blown — and the apparent meaning is that it is the second blast — there will be no kinship among them that Day. It is asked: what is the meaning of negating kinship among them, given that it remains, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the Deafening Blast comes, the Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his wife and his children﴾ [Abasa: 33–36]? So in this verse kinship among them is affirmed.

The second question: He said ﴿nor will they ask one another﴾, although He mentioned in other verses that they will ask one another in the Hereafter, such as His saying in Surat at-Tur: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ [at-Tur: 25], and His saying in as-Saffat: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ [as-Saffat: 27], and other verses besides these.

We have mentioned the answer to these two questions in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" with the following essential content:

The answer to the first question is that the intended meaning of the negation of kinship is the cessation of its effects which were consequential upon it in the worldly life: of pride in fathers, of benefit, of affections and of ties. All of that will cease on the Day of Resurrection, and a person will be concerned with nothing but himself. The intended meaning is not the negation of the reality of kinship from its root, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿The Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father﴾ [Abasa: 34–35], and so on.

The answer to the second question has three aspects:

The first: it is the saying of one who said: the negation of questioning is after the first blast and before the second, and its affirmation is after both together. This answer, as it appears, is not free from scrutiny.

The second: that the negation of questioning is at the time when they are occupied with the swoon and the reckoning and the crossing over the Sirat, and its affirmation is in other than that. This is from as-Suddi, through the chain of 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that the negated questioning is a specific questioning, namely one of them asking another for pardon regarding the rights existing between them, due to their despair of being given anything, even if the one asked were a father, a son, a mother or a wife. The scholar of al-Itqan mentioned these three aspects.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask one another.﴾

This noble verse indicates that there will be no kinship among them on that Day, and that they will not ask one another on the Day of (p-351) Resurrection. Other verses have come indicating the affirmation of kinship among them, such as His saying: ﴿The Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [80], and other verses indicate that they will ask one another, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ [as-Saffat: 27].

As for the answer to the first: the intended meaning of the negation of kinship is the cessation of its benefits and effects which were consequential upon it in the worldly life: of affections, benefit, ties and pride in fathers, not the negation of its reality.

As for the answer to the second, it has three aspects:

The first: that the negation of questioning is after the first blast and before the second, and its affirmation after both together.

The second: that the negation of questioning is at the time when they are occupied with the swoon, the reckoning and the crossing over the Sirat, and its affirmation is in other than that. This is from as-Suddi, through the chain of 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that the negated questioning is a specific questioning, namely one of them asking another for pardon regarding the rights existing between them, due to their despair of being given anything, even if the one asked were a father, a son, a mother or a wife. The scholar of al-Itqan also mentioned these three aspects.

Allah's statement: ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost their souls, abiding forever in Hell.﴾ I have already presented the clarifying verses explaining the meaning of these two verses in Surat al-A'raf, in the discussion of His statement: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth. Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful. And whoever's scales are light...﴾ [al-A'raf: 8-9], and His statement in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿Indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Kahf: 105], and other than that, so that suffices in place of repeating it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces, and they will be grimacing therein.﴾ What He mentioned in this noble verse is that the disbelievers' faces will be scorched by the Fire, meaning it will burn them severely. This is made clear in other places, such as:

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾ [al-Ahzab: 66],

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾ [al-Naml: 90],

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew the time when they will not be able to keep the Fire from their faces or from their backs...﴾ [al-Anbiya: 39],

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their garments will be of pitch, and the Fire will cover their faces﴾ [Ibrahim: 50],

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then is one who will shield his face from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [al-Zumar: 24],

• And His saying: ﴿It scalds the faces; wretched is the drink﴾ [al-Kahf: 29],

along with other verses.

As for His saying: ﴿and they will be grimacing therein﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 104], al-kalih (كالِح) is the one whose lips have drawn back until his teeth show. The Fire, we seek refuge in God, burns their lips until they pull back from their teeth, just as this can be observed in the head of a roasted sheep placed in a very hot fire. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

He has the foremost position, with no one equal to him, at the moment when the cheek pulls back from the fang and the face is grimacing (kalih).

And from Ibn 'Abbas: kalihun means frowning (ʿabisun).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 105:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Were My verses not recited to you, and did you not deny them?﴾ ﴿They said: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a misguided people."﴾ (p-358) What He, exalted and most high, mentioned in this noble verse is that the people of the Fire will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection, and their Lord will say to them: "Were My verses not recited to you," i.e., in the worldly abode, upon the tongues of the Messengers, "and did you not deny them?" And they admitted to that, and that they did not respond to the Messengers when they invited them to faith. This is because Allah willed wretchedness for them, and they were facilitated toward what they were created for, and therefore they disbelieved and denied the Messengers.

We have already clarified the verses that indicate this in Surah Bani Isra'il, in discussing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a Messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15], so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

As for His saying here: ﴿They said: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a misguided people."﴾ The apparent meaning of their saying "our wretchedness overcame us" is that the Messengers conveyed to them, warned them, and recited to them the verses of their Lord, but what had preceded in Allah's knowledge of their eternal wretchedness prevailed over them, so they denied the Messengers, in order to arrive at what had preceded in His knowledge, exalted and most high, of their wretchedness. A parallel to the verse in this sense is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ ﴿Even if every sign should come to them until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus 96-97], and His saying about the people of the Fire: ﴿They will say, "Yes, but the word of punishment has been justified against the disbelievers"﴾ [az-Zumar 71], and other verses besides. What further clarifies this is His saying ﷺ: "Each is facilitated for what he was created for," and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is the One who created you, and among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [at-Taghabun 2], and His saying: ﴿And they will continue to differ, ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them﴾ [Hud 118-119], according to the more correct of the two interpretations. And His saying about them, ﴿and we were a misguided people﴾, is their admission of their error, where admission of sin and regret for it will not benefit, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they will admit their sin, so away with the companions of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk 11], and similar verses.

This which we have explained the verse by is the most apparent meaning, which the Book and the Sunnah indicate. By it you will know that the saying of Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qurtubi in the explanation of this verse, "and the best of what has been said in its meaning: our desires and our appetites overcame us, so he named the pleasures and the appetites 'wretchedness,' because they lead to it, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [an-Nisa' 10]; because that leads them to the Fire." End of quote, is a far-fetched interpretation that contradicts the careful verification.

Then al-Qurtubi related what we mentioned as the correct view with one opinion, then said: "And it has been said: good opinion of oneself and bad opinion of creation." End of quote.

There is no doubt that the correct view is what we have mentioned, God willing. And His saying here: ﴿a misguided people﴾ (p-359) means: astray from Islam to disbelief, and from the path of Paradise to the path of the Fire. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this word as "shaqawatuna" with a fatha on the shin, and the qaf followed by an alif after it, while the rest read it with a kasra on the shin, a sukun on the qaf, and the alif omitted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 107:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾ ﴿He said, "Remain in it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ In this noble verse, the Majestic and Exalted mentions that the people of the Fire will call upon their Lord therein, saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return﴾ to what does not please You after our being brought out of it, then indeed we are wrongdoers. And Allah answers them with His words: ﴿Remain in it, and do not speak to Me.﴾ That is: remain therein as ones who are cast out (khasi'in), i.e., humiliated, debased and despised. For the word ukhsa' (be cast out) is only said to one who is contemptible and abject, like a dog and the like. So His words ﴿Remain in it﴾ mean: be abased therein, abiding in lowliness and disgrace.

This exit from the Fire which they sought, the Most High has made clear that they will not attain it;

• like His words ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it, and theirs is a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 37]

• and His words: ﴿Thus will Allah show them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will not come out of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167]

• and His words: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it from anguish, they will be returned into it﴾ — the verse [al-Hajj: 22],

• and His words: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ [as-Sajdah: 20]

and other verses besides these.

The Qur'an has also given multiple answers to the request of the people of the Fire. Here they said: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it,﴾ and they were answered: ﴿Remain in it, and do not speak to Me.﴾ In as-Sajdah: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us and we will do righteousness﴾ [as-Sajdah: 12], and they were answered: ﴿But the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell..."﴾ — the verse [as-Sajdah: 13]. In Surah al-Mu'min: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice and given us life twice, and we have acknowledged our sins, so is there any way to exit?"﴾ [Ghafir: 11], and they were answered: ﴿That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved, but when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Greatest﴾ [Ghafir: 12]. In az-Zukhruf: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us!"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 77], and they were answered: ﴿Indeed, you will remain﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 77]. In Surah Ibrahim: ﴿Those who did wrong will say, "Our Lord, delay us to a near term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers"﴾ [Ibrahim: 44], and they are answered: ﴿Did you not swear before that there would be for you no cessation?﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. In Surah Fatir: ﴿And they will cry out therein, "Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteousness, other than what we used to do"﴾ [Fatir: 37], and they are answered (p-360): ﴿Did We not give you lives long enough for whoever would be reminded to be reminded? And there came to you the warner. So taste, for the wrongdoers have no helper﴾ [an-Najm: 37]; and other verses indicating similar answers.

And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas that between each request from it and its answer there is a thousand years, and Allah knows best. His words in this verse, ﴿and do not speak to Me,﴾ mean: concerning the lifting of the punishment from you, nor bringing you out of the Fire. May Allah protect us and our Muslim brothers from it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 109:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who used to say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ ﴿But you took them in mockery until they made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them.﴾

It has been established in the principles (usul al-fiqh) in the method of indication and alerting (al-ima' wa al-tanbih) that inna (indeed) with a kasra and a shadda is among the particles of causation (huruf al-ta'lil), as in your saying: "Punish him, indeed he is a wrongdoer," meaning: because of his wrongdoing. His saying in this verse, ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants﴾, shows through the wording of inna with a kasra and shadda that the causes which brought them into the Fire were their mockery and ridicule of the believing group who say: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful.﴾ So the disbelievers used to mock the weak among the believers in this world, until that caused them to forget the remembrance of Allah and faith in Him, and thereby they entered the Fire.

What He, exalted is He, mentioned in these two noble verses has been indicated elsewhere, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. And when they passed by them, they would wink at one another.﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29-30] And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We tested some of them by means of others, that they might say, "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?"﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 53]. All of that is contempt from them towards them, and their denial that Allah bestows any good upon them. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy?﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-A'raf: 49], and His saying, exalted is He, concerning them: ﴿If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11]. All of that is contempt from them towards them.

His saying: ﴿So you took them in mockery﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 110]. The sukhriyy, with a damma or a kasra, is the verbal noun of sakhira minhu, when one ridicules him in a manner of contempt. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding the ya' of nisba: it is an increase in the verb, as it is said of al-khususiyya with the meaning of al-khusus. Its meaning is that the doubled ya' at its end indicates an increase in their mockery of them and their exaggeration in that. Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read sukhriyyan with a damma on the sin, and the rest read it with a kasra, and the meanings of the two readings are one, namely the mockery and ridicule of the disbelievers toward the weak among the believers, as we have explained. Among those who said that their meanings are one are al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and this is the truth, if Allah, exalted is He, wills. From al-Kisa'i and al-Farra': that sikhriyy with a kasra on the sin is of the kind of ridicule we mentioned, and that sukhriyy with a damma on the sin is from taskhir, which is subjugation and servitude.

(p-361) The meaning is: the disbelievers subjugate the weak believers and enslave them, as Umayya ibn Khalaf used to do to Bilal. It is not hidden that the correct view is what we have mentioned, if Allah, exalted is He, wills. As for "until" (hatta) in His saying: ﴿until they made you forget My remembrance﴾, it is a particle of limit, relating to their taking them in mockery; that is, they continued to do so until that made them forget the remembrance of Allah and faith in Him, so their abode was the Fire, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they patiently endured; indeed, they are the triumphant﴾. In this noble verse, He - exalted is He and high is He - mentions that He rewarded those believers who were oppressed in the world with success (al-fawz) in Paradise in the Hereafter. His saying ﴿for what they patiently endured﴾ means: because of their patience in the abode of the world, against the harm of the disbelievers who took them as objects of mockery (sikhriyyan), and against other things such as complying with the command of Allah and avoiding His prohibitions. What this noble verse indicates, that those oppressed ones whom the disbelievers used to mock, Allah rewarded on the Day of Resurrection with success in His Garden and His good pleasure, has been explained in other places, along with the clarification that on the Day of Resurrection they will mock the disbelievers and laugh at them, while the disbelievers are in the Fire, and we seek refuge in Allah.

- As in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers, reclining on couches, looking on. Have the disbelievers been repaid for what they used to do?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 34-35]

- And His saying: ﴿Are these the ones you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy? Enter Paradise; no fear will be upon you, nor will you grieve﴾ [al-A'raf: 49]

- And His saying: ﴿The worldly life has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe. But those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Baqarah: 212]

And other verses besides these. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿innahum hum al-fa'izun﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah of inna. On both of their readings, the object of jaza-ytuhum is omitted, meaning: "I rewarded them with My Garden; indeed they are the triumphant." On this reading, inna is for beginning a new statement (isti'naf). The rest read ﴿annahum hum al-fa'izun﴾ with a fathah on the hamzah of anna. On the majority's reading, the verbal noun formed from anna and its complement is the direct object of jaza-ytuhum, meaning: "I rewarded them their triumph," as is well known. Al-fawz (triumph) is attaining the greatest sought-after goal.

The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 112:

Allah's words: ﴿He will say, "How many years did you remain on the earth?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "We remained a day or part of a day, so ask those who count."﴾ In this verse there is a well-known question. When they are asked on the Day of Resurrection about the length of their stay on earth in the world, they answer that they remained a day or part of a day. Yet other verses show that they gave answers other than this one, such as His saying: ﴿They will consult among themselves in whispers, "You remained but ten"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 103], and ten is more than a day or part of a day. And His saying: ﴿On the day the Hour comes, the criminals will swear that they remained not but an hour﴾ [al-Rum: 55], and an hour is less than a day or part of a day. And His saying: ﴿It is as if they had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 46]. And His saying: ﴿As if they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another﴾ [Yunus: 45]. And His saying: ﴿They remained but an hour of a day, a proclamation. Will any be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35].

We have explained the answer to this question in our book Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book) in the discussion of this verse, and its essence is as follows: some of them say, "We remained a day or part of a day," some of them say, "We remained an hour," and others among them say, "We remained ten."

The evidence for this answer from the Qur'an is that He, exalted is He, showed that the most perceptive of them, the soundest in intellect, and the most correct in their way, is the one who says that they remained only one day. This is in His saying: ﴿They will consult among themselves in whispers, "You remained but ten." We know best what they say when the most correct in their way says, "You remained not but a day."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 103–104]. So the verse is explicit that their statements differed, and on this basis there is no difficulty, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

As for His saying: ﴿so ask those who count﴾, meaning: those who calculate, who keep account of the length of our stay. Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read it by transferring the vowel of the hamzah to the sin and dropping the hamzah, while the rest read fas'al without transfer. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read qul kam labithtum (say, "How long did you remain?") with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the lam, in the imperative form. The rest read qala kam labithtum (he said, "How long did you remain?") with a fatha on the qaf, followed by an alif, and a fatha on the lam, in the past tense form.

Al-Zamakhshari said, in essence, that on the reading qala in the past tense, the subject is a pronoun referring to Allah, or to whoever among the angels was commanded to question them. On the reading qul in the imperative, the pronoun refers to the angel commanded to question them, or to some of the leaders of the people of the Fire. This is what he said, and Allah knows best.

Allah, exalted is He, has affirmed the truth of their claim about the brevity of their stay in the world in His saying: ﴿He will say, "You remained but a little, if only you had known."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 114].

This is because the period of their stay in the world is very short indeed, in comparison with the length of their eternal abiding in the Fire, and we seek refuge in Allah. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read qul in 'in labithtum illa qalilan (say, "You remained but a little") in the imperative form, while the rest read it in the past tense form.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 113:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will say, "We remained a day or part of a day, so ask those who keep count."﴾

This noble verse indicates that the disbelievers claim on the Day of Resurrection that they remained only a day or part of a day. Other verses have come which are understood to convey the opposite, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will whisper among themselves, "You remained not except ten [days]."﴾ [20:102], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they remained not except an hour.﴾ [30:55].

The answer to this is by what the Qur'an indicates, namely that some of them say: ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. Some of them say: "We remained an hour," and some of them say: "We remained ten [days]."

The way the Qur'an indicates this is that it made clear that the one with the strongest understanding, the soundest intellect and the best way (of thinking) among them is the one who says that the duration of their stay was a day, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When their best in way would say, "You remained not except a day."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 104]. This indicates the difference in their statements regarding the duration of their stay, and Allah knows best.

(p-363) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did you then think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ The interrogative in His saying "Did you then think" is for denunciation (al-inkar). Here, al-husban (reckoning, supposition) means al-zann (thinking, supposing). That is: "Did you suppose that We created you in vain, without wisdom, and that you would not be returned to Us on the Day of Resurrection, so that We would recompense you for your deeds — if good, then good, and if evil, then evil?" Then He, exalted is He, declared Himself free of (tanzih) the notion that their creation was in vain, and that they would not return to Him for reckoning and recompense.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 116:

And His saying: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth. There is no deity except Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ Meaning: He is magnified and sanctified, and transcendent above everything that is not befitting to His perfection and majesty. Among that is that He created you in vain. Glorified is He and Exalted, high above that with a great highness.

What this verse includes of the denial of the aforementioned assumption has been clarified in other places,

such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and that between them in vain. That is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾ [Sad: 27]

and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and that between them in play. We did not create them except with truth﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 38-39]

and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected? Was he not a sperm-drop from semen emitted? Then he was a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned, and made of him two sexes, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36-39]. His saying "neglected" (sudan) means: left without being brought to account or recompensed, and it is the place of denying that assumption in His saying: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾

As for His saying "in vain" (abathan): it may be parsed as a circumstantial accusative (hal), since it is an indefinite verbal noun (masdar), meaning: We created you only while We were playing. It may also be parsed as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), meaning: We created you only for the sake of vanity, not for a wisdom that required Our creating you. Some have parsed it as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), but this is not apparent. Al-Qurtubi said: "Abathan" means: heedless, and "abath" in the language means play. What indicates its interpretation in this verse as play is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and that between them in play﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 38], and His saying: ﴿the King, the Truth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 116]. Some said: that is, the One to whom sovereignty is due, because everything is from Him and returns to Him. Others said: "the King, the Truth" means the Established, whose sovereignty never ceases, as we previously explained in Surat an-Nahl in discussing His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Him belongs religion, constant﴾ [an-Nahl: 52].

The Throne was described as "noble" only because of its greatness and the magnitude of its station. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿and that you to Us will not be returned﴾ is conjoined with His saying: ﴿that We created you in vain.﴾ This is contrary to one who said it is conjoined with His saying "in vain," because the first is more apparent than it. And knowledge is with Allah, Exalted is He.

(p-364) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof, then his account is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾

Al-Burhan (proof): the evidence that leaves no ambiguity regarding the truth. His saying, "for which he has no proof" (la burhana lahu bihi) is like His saying: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that for which He has not sent down any authority﴾ [al-Hajj: 71]. Al-Sultan (authority) is the clear argument, and it has the same meaning as al-burhan. His saying in this noble verse, ﴿then his account is only with his Lord﴾, has made clear that his account, which is with his Lord, holds no success for him in it.

By His saying after it, ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ The greatest of disbelievers in disbelief is the one who calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof. The negation of success for him indicates his ruin and that he is among the people of the Fire. Allah has warned against calling upon another god along with Him in many verses,

such as His saying: ﴿And do not set up with Allah another god, lest you be cast into Hell, blameworthy and expelled﴾... [al-Dhariyat: 51 in the source reads: ﴿And do not make with Allah another god; indeed, I am to you a clear warner from Him﴾] [al-Dhariyat: 51]

and His saying: ﴿And do not call upon another god besides Allah. There is no deity except Him. Everything will perish except His face. To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]

and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not make with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken﴾ [al-Isra': 22]

The verses of this kind are very numerous, and there is no disagreement among the scholars of knowledge that His saying here, ﴿for which he has no proof﴾, does not carry an implied opposite meaning (mafhum al-mukhalafah). So it is not valid for anyone to say: as for one who worships along with Him another god for which he has a proof, there is no objection to that, since it is impossible for a proof to exist for worshipping another god along with Him. Rather, the definitive, mass-transmitted proofs indicate that He alone is the One worshipped, may He be majestic and exalted, and it is impossible that any evidence for worshipping other than Him should exist whatsoever.

It has been established in the discipline of usul al-fiqh (legal theory) that among the impediments to considering the implied opposite meaning (mafhum al-mukhalafah) is that the specification of an attribute by mention is due to its conformity with reality. The text thus mentions an attribute that conforms to reality so that the ruling may be applied to it. Its specification by mention is therefore not to exclude the implied meaning from the ruling of the explicit statement, but to specify the attribute by mention because it conforms to reality.

Among its examples in the Qur'an is this verse, because His saying ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is an attribute that conforms to reality, since they call upon another besides Him without any proof. So He mentioned the attribute because it conforms to reality, not to exclude the implied meaning from the ruling of the explicit statement.

Among its examples in the Qur'an also is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]; because it was revealed concerning a people who allied with the Jews instead of the believers. So His saying ﴿instead of the believers﴾ is a mention for conformity with reality, not to exclude the implied meaning from the ruling of the explicit statement. And it is known that taking the disbelievers as allies over the believers is forbidden in every case.

It was to this that the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud pointed when mentioning the impediments to considering the implied opposite meaning, in his verse:

"Or a favour, or conformity with reality, or ignorance, or emphasis in the listener's ear."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 23, verse 118:

His saying, may He be exalted, at the conclusion of this noble surah: ﴿And say, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ contains the evidence that those group of people who used to say: ﴿Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful﴾ [al-A'raf: 155] were granted success in their supplication, and for this reason Allah praised them for it, and He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to do the same so that his ummah would follow him in that. The object of "forgive" and "have mercy" is omitted here, because of the indication of what preceded it in His saying: ﴿So forgive us and have mercy upon us﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. Al-maghfirah (forgiveness) is the covering of sins through Allah's pardon and forbearance, to the point that no trace of them appears that would harm their owner. Al-rahmah (mercy) is an attribute of Allah from which He derived His name al-Rahman and His name al-Rahim, and it is an attribute whose effects appear upon His creatures whom He shows mercy to. The superlative form in His saying: ﴿and You are the best of the merciful﴾ is used because created beings may show mercy to one another, but there is no doubt that Allah's mercy differs from the mercy of His creation, just as His essence and the rest of His attributes differ from their essences and attributes, as we have clarified in Surat al-A'raf in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then He istawa (rose) over the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.
